docs.title: Arabic Security-Training Lure Deploying a VBA Reverse Shell
Introduction
docs.text:
In May 2026, I stumbled upon a weaponised Microsoft Word macro-enabled template (.dotm, 33,966 bytes, SHA-256 e6cc542b690066cf6914e88199ce234236f2d929f313af8b0b2f8babe43d4f7d) that surfaced through one of the VirusTotal hunting rule. The template carries an Arabic-language lure themed as a peer-to-peer review request for a "third security training course", stored as an AutoText entry rather than in the visible document body.

Exhibit 1: Lure Document

Its VBA project, on Document_Open, decodes a letter-encoded ASCII-triplet payload from a UserForm TextBox and attempts to inject it as new VBA into the user's Normal.dotm global template through the Office object model. The stage-2 reverse shell connects to 51.38.87.253:25255 and bound an interactive cmd.exe to the socket on every Document_Close. The IP 51.38.87.253 has been associated with APT42 / Charming Kitten (Iranian-nexus, also tracked as TA453, Mint Sandstorm, Yellow Garuda) infrastructure

docs.title: Lure Document Analysis
docs.text:
The lure is a one-page Arabic-language course brochure for a six-day private-security training programme, framed as a draft schedule that the author wants reviewed before delivery. It opens with the Islamic Basmala, then lays out a table of topics, timings, learning outcomes, and target beneficiaries - running from 9 AM to noon daily - covering the duties and attributes of a security guard, security awareness, body language and threat recognition, search techniques, dealing with different segments of society, emergency response, watchtower and alarm operation, radio communications, conflict management, risk assessment, dress and standing posture, VIP protection, security report writing, and "the ethics of Islam in security work." The intended audience is named explicitly: security personnel generally, facility/company/shop guards, residential guards, and anyone interested in the subject. It closes with the signature of "Mr. Maytham Al-Uraimi" - a name with Omani/Emirati Gulf-region resonance - which, combined with the Arabic.dotm template and the otherwise mundane, professionally-framed content, makes it look like a piece of legitimate Gulf private-security training material that was either authored by or scraped from a real practitioner and then repurposed as a social-engineering wrapper.

The sample is a Microsoft Word 2007+ macro-enabled template (.dotm), not a macro-enabled document (.docm). The [Content_Types].xml part-type override for word/document.xml is the canonical .dotm content type and the file's MIME identifier matches. Templates are loaded by Word into the global template chain at session start and run their VBA on Document_Open for any document derived from them, which makes the template-format choice operationally meaningful: the malicious VBA runs in a slightly different trust path from a regular .docm lure.

Exhibit 2: Document Metadata

The template's metadata reports Creator: Win10 (the Word-internal application-creator identifier left at a generic value, not a typed operator persona) and Last Modified By: Kristina Rowell.

The metadata timestamps place the template's authoring window in February 2022, with a Create Date of 2022-02-06 12:21:00 UTC, a Modify Date of 2022-02-09 14:30:00 UTC, 13 recorded revisions, and a total edit time of one minute. The sample landed in the VirusTotal hunting queue in May 2026 and uploaded from Bangladesh, leaving a ~4-year gap between authoring and observed delivery. Either the operator is using a long-reused tooling artifact, or the metadata timestamps are spoofed, both are plausible.

A second, stronger temporal signal is the ZIP archive's per-entry modification dates. Every one of the 20 OOXML parts inside the .dotm is timestamped 1980-01-01 00:00:00, the DOS-time epoch zero. Microsoft Word does not produce this — when Word saves a .dotm, each part receives a real Zip Modify Date. A uniform epoch-zero stamp across every entry means the OOXML container was re-packed by an external tool after Word built it, typically a Python zipfile.ZipInfo(..., date_time=(1980,1,1,0,0,0)) builder or a similar weaponisation helper. This is evidence of a build pipeline, not of an operator clicking "Save" in Word.

Exhibit 3: ZIP Listing Showing all 20 Entries Pinned to 1980-01-01 00:00:00 - the File was Re-packaged Outside Word.

docs.title: VBA Project Analysis
docs.text:
The VBA project (word/vbaProject.bin, 34,816 bytes) is the legacy OLE2 wrapper Office still uses for VBA inside OOXML. Static triage with oleid reports a high-risk VBA project with suspicious indicators.

Exhibit 4: oleid Triage Output

The OLE2 project contains ten streams across two code modules: VBA/ThisDocument (the dropper) and VBA/UserForm1 (a near-empty code-behind for the UserForm that holds the encoded payload). The oledump.py -i listing splits each M-flagged code stream into compiled p-code and compressed source; ThisDocument carries 4611 + 1630 bytes (p-code + source) and UserForm1 carries 1045 + 274.

Exhibit 5: VBA Stream Layout

docs.title: Macro Execution Chain
docs.text:
Further analysis revealed that Document_Open is the only autoexec hook (vbaData.xml: <wne:eventDocOpen/>; project name TemplateProject). It sets view to wdPrintView, unprotects with the hard-coded password 20exlnt20, sets alreadyLaunched = True, and calls Launch. alreadyLaunched is never declared at module scope, so VBA gives each sub its own implicit procedure-local Variant; Launch's gating check fails against a fresh local and execution continues into SubstitutePage and Create_Word.

SubstitutePage replaces the (empty) body with the AutoText entry Doc from the attached Arabic.dotm template and saves.

Create_Word writes HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Office\16.0\Word\Security\AccessVBOM = 1 to permit VBA self-modification, decodes the 16,392-character letter-encoded payload from UserForm1.TextBox1.Text via Putin (letter-to-digit substitution a → 0 … j → 9, then Chr(...) over each three-digit group; 5,464 bytes of VBA out), instantiates a hidden Word.Application (Visible = 0, DisplayAlerts = 0), creates a transient document via Documents.Add(""), and calls doc.VBProject.VBComponents(1).CodeModule.AddFromString (Putin(content)) to inject the decoded VBA into that transient document's ThisDocument module. It then closes the transient document with no SaveChanges (suppressed by DisplayAlerts = 0), quits the hidden app, and chains into unlink. The transient document never reaches disk; the stage-2 VBA does not survive Create_Word's return.

unlink is the apparent persistence move and does not work as intended. It reassigns ActiveDocument.AttachedTemplate from Arabic.dotm to C:\Users\<UserName>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Templates\Normal.dotm (resolved via Application.UserName), saves the lure, and closes it. This is a pointer change on the lure's attached-template property; it does not copy VBA code between projects, and Normal.dotm is not modified. DeleteVBAPROJECT (the component-wipe) is reachable only via unlink's On Error GoTo Destroy guard; on a clean execution Exit Sub returns first and the wipe never runs. The lure on disk ends up with its AttachedTemplate pointer redirected to Normal.dotm and its own VBA project intact.

Net effect: AccessVBOM = 1, lure body replaced with the Arabic decoy, attached-template pointer moved to Normal.dotm, lure re-saved and closed. The stage-2 reverse shell is constructed but not persisted and not executed. The chain does not, as written, achieve the apparent operator intent; runtime confirmation would settle whether a Word internal quirk inherits the transient document's VBProject into Normal.dotm despite the discard.

docs.title: UserForm Payload Extraction and Decoding
docs.text:
The stage-2 substrate lives in the UserForm1/o OLE stream of word/vbaProject.bin, 16,448 bytes long. This stream is not opaque binary - it is two concatenated MS-OFORMS TextProps records, each carrying one of the UserForm's variable-length property values. Walking the stream as (2-byte Version | 2-byte cbTextProps | Body) produces a clean partition: a 16,420-byte record at offset 0x0000 carrying the TextBox's Text property (the encoded payload), followed immediately by a 28-byte record at offset 0x4024 carrying the TextBox's FontName property (the string Tahoma). Total consumed: 16,420 + 28 = 16,448 bytes, the entire stream. The payload itself (a single contiguous block of [a-j] characters, 16,392 bytes long) sits inside the larger record's ExtraDataBlock, beginning at stream offset 0x001C and ending at 0x4024 immediately before the second record's header.

Exhibit 7: xxd -l 64 /tmp/UserForm1_o.bin and xxd -s -64 /tmp/UserForm1_o.bin side-by-side, showing the OFORMS header 00 02 20 40 … at offset 0x00 resolving into the [a-j] payload at 0x1C, and the trailing TextProps record 00 02 18 00 … at 0x4024 containing the Tahoma font value.

Decoding the payload statically reproduces what Putin would output at runtime. The longest [a-j] run is exactly 16,392 characters, divisible by 3, yielding 5,464 triplets with no out-of-range values. The first three triplets decode to 067 111 110 (C, o, n) and the last three to 083 117 098 (S, u, b); the recovered file therefore begins with Const ip = "51.38.87.253" and ends with End Sub, exactly the start and end of a complete VBA module. The decoded module is 5,464 bytes; its SHA-256 is 317f6f93fe81d1800cbbb1d8f8dbb7c7b27412358f3058f58a2496bae20f0863.

Exhibit 8: Python decode harness output showing encoded len: 16392, decoded len: 5464, the SHA-256, first line Const ip = "51.38.87.253", and last line End Sub.

docs.title: Stage-2 Reverse-Shell Analysis
docs.text:
The decoded VBA module is 145 lines of Winsock reverse-shell code. It declares four Win32 structures (WSADATA, ADDRINFO, STARTUPINFOA, PROCESS_INFORMATION), two enums for address families and socket types, and ten Private Declare PtrSafe API imports from ws2_32.dll (WSAStartup, WSACleanup, WSAGetLastError, WSASocketA, connect, closesocket, GetAddrInfo) and kernel32.dll (CopyMemory, ZeroMemory, and CreateProc aliased to CreateProcessA). The C2 endpoint is hard-coded as VBA string constants at the top of the module: ip = "51.38.87.253" and port = "25255".

Exhibit 9: Stage-2 Winsock Reverse-shell Code

The revShell() function is the canonical Winsock-spawn-cmd reverse-shell pattern. It calls WSAStartup(MAKEWORD(2,2), ...) to initialise Winsock 2.2, resolves the C2 via GetAddrInfo with ai_family = AF_UNSPEC and ai_socktype = SOCK_STREAM, and walks the returned addrinfo linked list calling WSASocketA and connect for each node until one succeeds. Once connected, it zero-initialises a STARTUPINFOA, sets dwFlags = &H100 (STARTF_USESTDHANDLES), assigns the connected socket handle to hStdInput, hStdOutput, and hStdError, and calls CreateProc(vbNullString, "cmd", ByVal 0&, ByVal 0&, True, &H8000000, 0, vbNullString, si, pi). The combination of bInheritHandles = TRUE and CREATE_NO_WINDOW (0x08000000) binds cmd.exe's standard handles to the connected socket while suppressing the console window. This is a textbook Windows reverse-shell construction.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
The dropper's intended mechanism is template-poisoning of %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Templates\Normal.dotm such that an injected Document_Close() would fire on every Word-document close. The chain does not achieve this. Create_Word injects the stage-2 VBA into the VBProject of a transient document, then immediately discards it:

Set doc = Wordy.Documents.Add("")             ' new transient document - its own VBProject
doc.VBProject.VBComponents(1).CodeModule.AddFromString (Putin(content))   ' code added to transient doc
doc.Close                                      ' transient doc discarded (DisplayAlerts=0 suppresses save prompt)

docs.title: Infrastructure and Attribution
docs.text:
The sample itself was submitted to VirusTotal a single time, from Bangladesh, on 10-05-2026.

The IP 51.38.87.253 has been associated with APT42 / Charming Kitten (Iranian-nexus, also tracked as TA453, Mint Sandstorm, Yellow Garuda) infrastructure, but I have not independently verified this association from the sample alone (https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/untangling-iran-apt42-operations).

The Arabic security-training-course lure theme is compatible with APT42 / Charming Kitten targeting (Iranian-nexus actors have a documented history of operations against Arabic-speaking security and military entities across the Gulf, Iraq, Lebanon, and Syria), but theme alone does not constitute attribution.

NOTE: Weather this was an old sample uploaded just now by some researcher, or new potential APT42 campaign lure is beyond my current knowledge. In any case, it's was an interesting sample to analyse.

docs.title: A Five-Stage PowerShell HTTP RAT Hidden Behind an Employee Resume Lure
Summary
docs.text: In May 2026, I came across a macro-enabled Word document, EmployeeResumeForm.docm, hosted on the free-tier provider 42web[.]io and submitted to VirusTotal a few hours after creation. This report explains the document lure's construction, the five-stage PowerShell unwrap that hides its real payload, a scheduled task it installs for persistence, and the small custom HTTPS RAT that ultimately calls home.

docs.title: Key Highlights
docs.text:
• The initial-access vector is a macro-enabled .docm that reconstructs an encrypted PowerShell loader on disk from a array, then chains five layers of base64 and XOR before the real RAT executes.

  • The implant beacons roughly every 30 seconds (20% jitter, about ±6 seconds) to hxxps://updatepowershellservice[.]42web[.]io/YE97Bw999zB87t1U8i.php, supports four task primitives (cmd, powershell, file upload, file download), and persists through a scheduled task pretending to be a Microsoft Edge update job

docs.title: Lure Design and Targeting
docs.text:
The observed file is a 73,837-byte Microsoft Word 2007+ macro-enabled document, served from hxxps://dxi24-5wj3s-lsk32-j2o3s-aks3e[.]42web[.]io/EmployeeResumeForm.docm and reached via a mailstat[.]us tracking redirector. The randomised-token subdomain and the mail-tracker URL together suggested the document was distributed by email, although I did not recover the original carrier message.

Figure 1: Lure Document Observed during analysis

The lure name, an employee resume form, is unusually specific. Resume themes are most often used to target HR and recruitment staff who routinely open attachments from unknown senders. I considered whether the buildInfo value baesystem in the implant's encrypted config (recovered later in this report) indicates active targeting of BAE Systems' recruitment workflow.

Figure 2: Employee Resume Form after Enabling Macro

The document metadata reveals some interesting information. The file lists Mighty Spider as both the Creator and Last Modified By, with Microsoft Office Word as the originating application and Normal.dotm as the template - the same handle in both fields suggests the author did not bother to scrub identifying attributes between revisions. Total edit time is one minute over three revisions, and the file was created at 02:16 UTC and last saved at 02:42 UTC on 20 May 2026, with VirusTotal first-seen at 05:14 UTC the same day - a tight three-hour create-to-submit window consistent with on-demand weaponisation rather than reuse of a stale template.

Figure 3: Lure Document Metadata

docs.title: Delivery Mechanism
docs.text:
A .docm is an Office Open XML container, which is to say it is a ZIP archive. Unzipping it yields the usual OOXML scaffolding - word/document.xml, [Content_Types].xml, the docProps/ metadata folder - and one binary file that does not fit the XML pattern: word/vbaProject.bin. That single 60 KB blob is where every macro in the document lives.

Figure 4: Lure Document Internal Content Container

When Microsoft introduced OOXML in 2007, they kept the older Office binary format (a Compound File Binary, or "OLE structured storage" container) for macro storage and embedded the entire mini-filesystem unchanged inside the ZIP.1 So, vbaProject.bin is itself a structured archive: a PROJECT stream with project-level metadata, a dir stream listing the modules, and one stream per module (ThisDocument and Module1) each holding the original VBA source.

I decompressed the MS-OVBA block and printed a readable source dump resulting in around 870-line listing of what the .bin file represents.

Once the victim enables macros, the Document_Open handler in ThisDocument calls Module1.default and then runs DelAllShapesInDoc to walk ActiveDocument.Shapes and delete every shape on the page. The shape-wipe is a small but telling design choice. The lure's visible content disappears immediately after execution, removing the only obvious cue that the user would have noticed something change.

The reason why the author calls it after the loader fires could probably be treated as multi-purpose:

  • The victim clicked Enable Content expecting something to render. If the lure body was a "Document Preview / Enable editing to view full content" decoy graphic, wiping the shapes leaves them looking at a blank page. The natural human reaction is to close it, dismiss, move on. Meanwhile the loader has already dropped something and scheduled the recurring task.

  • If the user (or AutoRecover) saves the document after macros ran, the saved copy no longer contains the lure decoy or the "enable macros" prompt.

  • Sandbox screenshot defeat: Many automated sandboxes screenshot the document after detonation.

  • Defenders sometimes fingerprint lures on their embedded images (logo crops, decoy header art). Once the macro has run, those images are gone from the in-memory document object.

Module1.default is where the actual dropper logic lives. This file contains five steps that together rebuild an encrypted PowerShell loader on disk and hand execution to powershell.exe:

  • Instantiate a WScript.Shell COM object - the channel the macro will eventually use to spawn cmd.exe.

  • Declare the payload array: Dim payloadLines(35, 19) As String, with 710 of the 720 cells assigned literal strings of the form "Error: <base64 chunk>". The remaining ten cells are intentionally empty.

  • Reassemble the encrypted loader: a nested loop walks the 36 × 20 array in row-major order and concatenates the non-empty cells with vbCrLf into a single multi-line string - the body of the file that will become default.ps1.

  • Drop to disk: enableCNFV (a pure-VBA MkDir-based directory creator) ensures C:\Users\Public\Microsoft exists, then enableWFV (a pure-VBA Open ...For Output As fileNum + Print #fileNum writer) saves the assembled string to C:\Users\Public\Microsoft\default.ps1.

  • Spawn the loader: an eight-element psChunks array is concatenated into one long command line and handed to shell.Run longCmd, 0, True - window style 0 (hidden), wait flag True (blocking until the spawned process exits).

An explicit author comment Pure VBA version - no FileSystemObject required confirms that the dropper's evasion strategy is inconsistent across phases. For the file drop, the author sidesteps the COM-creation telemetry that AMSI providers and EDR hooks rely on by writing the file with native VBA primitives rather than Scripting.FileSystemObject or ADODB.Stream. While that effectively cloaks the file write, the evasion stops there: the subsequent execution path reverts to a heavily monitored COM scripting object (WScript.Shell) and leaves a clear behavioural footprint.

docs.title: Five-Stage PowerShell Loader Analysis
docs.text:
The macro leaves two artefacts behind, neither of them directly executable. The first is the file C:\Users\Public\Microsoft\default.ps1, whose every line begins with Error: and which, to a casual look, resembles a corrupted log file. The second is the in-memory PowerShell process that cmd.exe spawns, parameterised by the base64-encoded script body inside the $rukp variable on its command line. The file on disk is ciphertext. The script on the command line is the decryptor. The two are designed to fit together only at execution time.

To recover the malicious behaviour, I peeled away the wrappers in the order the malware itself would peel them. Between the base64 sitting on cmd.exe's command line and the final PowerShell HTTP RAT that beacons to the C2, there are five distinct unwrap operations. Each layer uses one of two primitives - a base64 decode, or an XOR against a mixed key - and each layer's output is the next layer's input:

  • Stage 1: outer cmdline base64

  • stage-2 PowerShell with Invoke-EnvironmentCheck + scheduled-task action

  • Stage 2: UTF-16LE -Enc base64 (the task's Argument)

  • $rukp = '<base64>'; iex wrapper

  • Stage 3: inner ASCII base64

  • decryptor: reads default.ps1, strips "Error:", base64+XOR, iex

  • Stage 4: default.ps1 XOR-decrypted with key:salt = E8/LNvsiT2w/IyTlSVyqPQ==:aYcZU4lHrxI=

  • mixed key 7a48d2657265e07e56a43db6c01b052f

  • yet another $rukp = '<base64>'; iex wrapper

  • Stage 5: inner base64

  • final HTTP RAT

docs.title: Stage-by-Stage Analysis
docs.text:
The macro hands an eight-chunk concatenated command line to shell.Run, and the -C argument is base64-encoded PowerShell wrapped in a $rukp = '<b64>'; iex-style dispatcher. Decoding that base64 produces a ~5,800-byte script with two visible halves: the Invoke-EnvironmentCheck function (the 50+ process anti-analysis routine analysed in the next section) and a Register-ScheduledTask block that installs the recurring four-hour persistence task. Stage 1 is the script that runs once, immediately after macro detonation, and whose sole job is to gate execution and arrange for the rest of the chain to run later.

Figure 5: Partial Representation of the Stage 1

The Register-ScheduledTask call in stage 1 sets the task action's Argument to powershell.exe -NoP -exec BYpass -w hIdden -Enc <base64>.

Stage 2 is not a payload in its own right - it is a thin trampoline that decodes the next layer at run time, every four hours, for as long as the task persists.

Figure 6: Base64 Blob Decoded from Stage 1 $action

Decoding the base64 inside stage 2's $rukp exposes the actual decryption logic. The script reads C:\Users\Public\Microsoft\default.ps1 from disk, strips the ^\w+:\s prefix from every line (the Error: masquerade), base64-decodes the remaining ciphertext, and XORs the result against a 16-byte mixed key derived from a hardcoded key:salt pair E8/LNvsiT2w/IyTlSVyqPQ==:aYcZU4lHrxI=*.

Figure 7: Partial Representation of the Stage 3

Running stage 3's logic against the on-disk default.ps1 produces 34,069 bytes of plaintext. The mixed-key construction is straightforward: a 16-byte key is XORed byte-by-byte against an 8-byte salt cycled to length 16, which for the dropper's key/salt yields the hex value 7a48d2657265e07e56a43db6c01b052f. The resulting plaintext is not yet the RAT but another IEX-style dispatcher, the same pattern that has appeared at every layer above it. By this point the author has used three nested base64 wrappers and one XOR layer to hide a fourth base64 wrapper.

Figure 8: Partial Representation of the Stage 4

Decoding stage 4's inner base64 finally yields executable PowerShell that is not itself a wrapper. The output is a ~25 KB script containing Get-UniqueDeviceId, Get-WanIP, Process-TaskCommands, Load-Config, the $gServerURL configuration handle and the Global\SysInfoProject_ mutex initialization. This is the RAT that beacons to the C2.

Figure 9: Partial Representation of the Stage 5

The implant's configuration, however, is encrypted inside the stage-5 script using the same XOR-mixed-key construction as the dropper - a different key:salt pair, an extra colon-delimited ciphertext field, and a separate mixed key (hex 1341c5c2cb57fc169984487a5aa1bc89). Decrypting it produces a single JSON object containing the C2 URL hxxps://updatepowershellservice.42web[.]io/YE97Bw999zB87t1U8i.php*, the implant's buildInfo tag baesystem, the spoofed Chrome 141 / Edg 141* user agent, the singleton mutex GUID and the sleep parameters.

Figure 10: Implant's Configuration

Stage 5 contains one further piece of code worth calling out here, because at a casual reading it looks like a sixth wrapper but is in fact a network helper. Inside the Invoke-Request function, and again inside the runspace initialiser that backs the implant's parallel uploader, the script defines a Get-Cookie routine that writes a JScript file named aes_<guid>.js into the user's %TEMP% directory and executes it with cscript.exe //nologo. The file is built at request time from two pieces fetched over the network: the slowAES JavaScript library served at /aes.js on the C2 host, and the HTML challenge page served at the C2 root. The implant strips the HTML wrapper and the location.href redirect tail from the page, substitutes WScript.Echo(toHex(slowAES.decrypt(c, 2, a, b))) for the redirect logic so that cscript prints the cookie value to standard output instead of navigating away, concatenates the two pieces into aes_<guid>.js, runs the file through cscript, and captures the resulting 32-character hex string. The string becomes the test cookie that the implant attaches to every subsequent MODE-headered POST, and a finally block removes the temporary file once cscript exits.

The reason this helper exists is that the C2 is hosted on InfinityFree, the free hosting platform behind the 42web[.]io domain, and InfinityFree fronts every customer site with a JavaScript anti-scraping check that requires the browser to solve a slowAES challenge before any further requests are accepted. Without a valid __test cookie, the C2 would reject the implant's POSTs as bot traffic, so the helper is a precondition for every C2 round trip rather than a stage in its own right. It does not appear in the five-layer unwrap above for the same reason: it does not wrap the next layer, it has no encoded body of its own, and its JavaScript content lives on the C2 rather than inside any of the stages on disk.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
Once the environment check passes, it installs a scheduled task whose action is C:\Windows\System32\conhost.exe with powershell.exe -NoP -exec BYpass -w hIdden -Enc <UTF-16LE base64> as its argument. The trigger is a one-off ten minutes after registration, repeating every four hours.

$action = New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute
"C:\Windows\System32\conhost.exe" `
-Argument "powershell.exe -NoP -exec BYpass -w hIdden -Enc
<b64>"
$trigger = New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Once -At (Get-Date).AddMinutes(10)
`
-RepetitionInterval (New-TimeSpan -Hours 4)
$stn = "MicrosoftEdgeUpdateTaskMachine-"
$stp = "Microsoft\Windows\TaskScheduler"
Register-ScheduledTask -TaskName ($stn +
([Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()).User.Value) `
-Action $action -Trigger $trigger -Force
try {
Register-ScheduledTask -TaskPath $stp `
-TaskName ($stn +
([Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()).User.Value) `
-Action $action -Trigger $trigger -Force `
-User "SYSTEM" -RunLevel Highest -ErrorAction Stop
} catch { }

Two design choices here are worth calling out. First, the task name is MicrosoftEdgeUpdateTaskMachine-<user SID>. Legitimate Microsoft Edge update tasks use a {GUID} suffix. Second, the loader registers the task twice: once in the user's own context, and then again under SYSTEM at -RunLevel Highest. The second call is wrapped in a try { ... } catch { } swallow, so on an unprivileged victim it silently fails and only the first registration sticks. On an admin or UAC-bypassed session, both succeed and the task runs as SYSTEM thereafter. That is the only privilege-escalation surface in the chain - there is no exploit, just an opportunistic attempt that costs nothing if it fails.

The third design detail is the choice of conhost.exe as the Execute argument with powershell.exe as its Argument. That trampoline forces conhost.exe to spawn powershell.exe as its child, which complicates simple parent-process detections that key on Office spawning PowerShell directly. The parent of the recurring PowerShell is therefore conhost, not cmd and not winword, and only the initial detonation produces the WINWORD -> cmd -> powershell tree.

docs.title: HTTPS RAT Capabilities
docs.text:
The final stage, recovered from default.ps1 after the XOR decrypt and the inner base64 unwrap, is a custom PowerShell HTTP RAT roughly 25 KB in size. I have not seen this loader's exact shape published elsewhere, and I refer to it by its own buildInfo value: baesystem.

The RAT's configuration lives encrypted in the script itself using the same XOR-mixed-key construction as the dropper, with a different key/salt pair and an extra colon-delimited ciphertext field: oUaJx2LlCscrgwR/8xNKWA==:sgdMBamy9tE=:<base64 ciphertext>.

Decrypting it yields a single JSON object.

{
"ServerURL":
"https://updatepowershellservice.42web.io/YE97Bw999zB87t1U8i.php",
"buildInfo": "baesystem",
"UserAgent": "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)
AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/141.0.0.0 Safari/537.36
Edg/141.0.0.0",
"mutexUID": "SysInfoProject_019d3efa-657d-73c5-b3d3-70a9a2ea5c39",
"sleepSecs": 30,
"sleepJitter": 20
}

updatepowershellservice[.]42web[.]io currently resolves to 185.27.134[.]177 (AS34119 Wildcard UK Limited), the IP that serves all of 42web[.]io's free-tier customers.

The C2 transport is HTTPS POSTs of JSON bodies carrying a custom MODE header. Five mode values appear in the source:

MODE value Direction Purpose LI victim -> C2 Initial login / registration of the beacon RP victim -> C2 Reports task results back to the operator GC victim -> C2 Polls the operator for queued commands UF victim -> C2 Uploads a file from the victim (exfiltration) DF victim -> C2 Pulls a file from the operator (ingress tool transfer)

The dispatcher Process-TaskCommands switches on a type field returned by the GC poll and supports exactly four task types: cmd (executed via cmd /c $taskCmd), powershell (executed via Invoke-Expression), download (calls Send-LargeFile to exfiltrate a file from victim to operator) and upload (calls Get-LargeFile to push a new file from operator to victim). The task-type names are written from the operator's perspective, which is the inverse of the victim-side MODE names: the download task exfiltrates from victim to operator and is carried by the UF (upload file) mode, while the upload task delivers a file from operator to victim and is carried by the DF (download file) mode.

docs.title: Detection and Mitigation
docs.text: I recommend the following layered approach to prevention, detection, and hunting:

docs.title: Prevention and Hardening
docs.text:
• Macro Restrictions: Block macro execution in documents originating from outside the organisation. Verify that Microsoft's Mark-of-the-Web (MotW) macro-blocking GPOs are strictly enforced.

  • PowerShell Constraints: Restrict PowerShell to Constrained Language Mode (CLM) for non-administrative users and verify that AMSI providers remain attached and functional.

docs.title: Host-Based Detection
docs.text:
• Malicious Execution Chains: Alert on a WINWORD.EXE ancestor spawning a cmd.exe → powershell.exe chain where the command line contains -NoP, -exec BYpass, -w hIdden, and a base64 argument exceeding three kilobytes in length.

  • Suspicious Scheduled Tasks (Naming): Alert on the creation of scheduled tasks named MicrosoftEdgeUpdateTaskMachine-S-1-5-*. The legitimate Edge updater uses a {GUID} suffix; the presence of a user SID is a high-fidelity anomaly.

  • Suspicious Scheduled Tasks (Execution): Alert on scheduled-task actions where the Execute target is conhost.exe and the Argument starts with powershell.exe. This trampoline technique is highly irregular for native Windows scheduled tasks.

  • Masqueraded File Drops: Alert on the creation of any file under C:\Users\Public\ whose first line matches the regex ^[A-Za-z]+:\s+[A-Za-z0-9+/]{40,}={0,2}$. The Error: <base64> masquerade is distinctive, and benign software does not produce this pattern.

docs.title: Network-Based Detection
docs.text:
• Custom HTTP Headers: Hunt and alert on outbound HTTPS POST traffic carrying a MODE request header with the values LI, RP, GC, UF, or DF. This is not a standard HTTP convention and should yield a near-zero noise hunt.

  • C2 Infrastructure: Block egress traffic to updatepowershellservice[.]42web[.]io. Consider blocking the wider *.42web[.]io namespace if business requirements permit.

docs.title: Threat Hunting
docs.text: • Mutex Sweeps: Hunt for the Global\SysInfoProject_* mutex using EDR telemetry (specifically querying for CreateMutex API calls) or by conducting live sweeps across the fleet using tools like handle.exe.

docs.title: Detection Efforts
docs.text:
To validate the detection logic recommended above, I detonated EmployeeResumeForm.docm on an instrumented sandbox shipping Elastic Defend into Elastic SIEM (with Sysmon present for the first detonation). This section documents what surfaced in Elastic SIEM, and which rules the telemetry would alert on.

Figure 11: Execution Chain Observed in Elastic SIEM

The sample was detonated in two phases. In the first phase the sandbox ran with Sysmon and standard VirtualBox guest tooling present. Under these conditions the malicious document spawned its initial process chain, but the embedded PowerShell terminated early without establishing persistence or contacting external infrastructure. Analysis of the deobfuscated script explained this behaviour. Before taking any action, the loader enumerates running processes and compares them against a hardcoded list of analysis, virtualisation, and forensic tooling, and it exits silently if any match is found. The presence of Sysmon alone was sufficient to trigger this check.

In the second phase the sandbox was re-provisioned with the Sysmon service and VirtualBox helper processes removed, so the sample would proceed past its environment check. This run produced the complete attack chain, including scheduled task persistence, a second execution stage, and command and control traffic. Elastic Defend retained full process, file, network, and registry visibility throughout both phases because its sensor does not run under any of the process names the sample screens for. The alerts and detection gaps described below are drawn from this second, fully executed run unless stated otherwise.

Across the fully executed run, Elastic Defend generated alerts from ten distinct detection rules. These fired at each major stage of the attack, from the initial document execution through to the command-and-control (C2) beacon. The table below consolidates them, grouped by the stage of the chain they covered.

Stage Rule Severity Coverage Initial execution Suspicious MS Office Child Process Medium Word spawning cmd.exe Initial execution Suspicious Windows Powershell Arguments Medium Hidden, encoded, execution-bypass PowerShell Discovery Deprecated - PowerShell Script with Discovery Capabilities Low Script reconnaissance behavior Persistence A scheduled task was created Low Scheduled task registration Stage 3 execution Unusual Parent-Child Relationship Medium conhost.exe spawning powershell.exe Discovery External IP Lookup from Non-Browser Process Low api.ipify.org request Discovery System Public IP Discovery via DNS Query High api.ipify.org request Command and control Remote File Download via PowerShell Medium C2 lookup and script drop Discovery Deprecated - Unusual Discovery Activity by User Low Anomalous discovery activity Discovery Unusual Discovery Signal Alert with Unusual Process Executable Low Anomalous discovery activity

The most important observation from this set is that detection coverage was broad but shallow, and the severities were inverted relative to the actual risk. The single High severity alert fired on the public IP lookup, which is a comparatively low-impact reconnaissance step.

The genuinely significant behaviours, namely the scheduled task persistence and the command-and-control activity, surfaced only as Low and Medium alerts. The alerts also arrived as isolated, single-event detections with no correlation between them, so an analyst would have seen a scatter of unrelated low-confidence signals rather than one coherent high-confidence incident. This fragmentation, combined with the inverted severity, is the central weakness this exercise exposed, and it directly motivates the new and tuned detections proposed in the next subsection.

docs.title: Detection Gaps and Recommended Rules
docs.text:
While the existing rule set produced alerts at most stages of the chain, several of the most security-relevant behaviours generated no alert at all. These gaps matter because they represent the techniques an analyst would most want flagged, and because they are the steps least likely to be benign in a production environment. The following behaviours were observed in the telemetry but did not trigger any detection rule.

The first gap is the use of cscript.exe to execute a JScript file from a user-writable temporary directory. On every C2 round trip the implant's Get-Cookie helper wrote a JScript file (aes_<guid>.js) into the user's %TEMP% directory and executed it through the Windows Script Host (cscript.exe //nologo), which breaks the PowerShell process lineage and continues execution under a different interpreter. No rule covered a script interpreter launching a script from a temporary or public path, despite this being a reliable indicator of staged execution.

The second gap is the use of conhost.exe as a proxy launcher. The scheduled task action invoked conhost.exe with powershell.exe and an encoded command as its arguments, using the console host as an intermediary to launch the payload. While an unusual parent-child rule did fire on the resulting relationship, no rule specifically identified conhost.exe being supplied another executable as an argument, which is an anomalous and high-confidence signal.

The third gap is the scheduled task masquerade. Persistence was registered under a task named to impersonate a legitimate Microsoft Edge update task, while its action pointed to an encoded PowerShell command rather than the genuine updater binary. The generic scheduled task creation rule did fire, but only at Low severity and without regard to the deceptive naming or the mismatch between the task name and its action. A detection that keys on this name and action mismatch would be both higher fidelity and higher severity.

The fourth gap is the malicious document writing a script to disk. The macro dropped a PowerShell script into a world-readable location under the Public user profile before execution began. No rule flagged an Office application writing a script or executable file type, even though Office processes have no legitimate reason to author such files in normal use.

The fifth gap is the sandbox and security tooling discovery performed by the loader. Before proceeding, the script enumerated running processes and compared them against an extensive list of virtualisation, debugging, and forensic tools. This is the behaviour that suppressed the first detonation entirely, and it is among the most distinctive signatures of this sample, yet nothing detected it. Capturing this reliably depends on PowerShell script block logging, which is addressed as a visibility gap below.

The sixth gap is the command-and-control (C2) beacon to free hosting infrastructure. The second stage resolved and connected to a domain on a free web hosting provider, and the repeated connections to the same destination indicated beaconing behaviour. The existing remote file download rule fired on the associated activity, but there was no detection keyed on a script interpreter contacting free or anomalous hosting infrastructure, and no analytic identifying the periodic beacon pattern itself.

Underlying several of these gaps is a visibility limitation rather than a missing rule. Elastic Defend observed only the outer command lines of the PowerShell stages, so the decrypted script bodies, the environment check logic, and the decryption routine were never available to the detection engine. Enabling PowerShell script block logging and ingesting it into Elastic SIEM is the single highest-value improvement available here, because it would expose the deobfuscated script content that rules five and the reflection-based loader behaviour depend on. This should be treated as a prerequisite for the script-content detections rather than an optional enhancement.

Taken together, these gaps share a common theme. The existing rules detect well-known atomic techniques such as Office spawning a shell or PowerShell using encoded arguments, but they do not cover the evasion, masquerade, and staging behaviours that distinguish this sample from commodity activity. The recommended rules below are designed to close those gaps, and to favour the behaviours that are both high fidelity and difficult for the actor to alter without changing their tradecraft.

docs.title: MuddyWater Weaponizes Word Macros in Targeted Campaign Delivering GhostFetch
MuddyWater Weaponises Word Macros in Targeted Campaign Delivering GhostFetch
docs.text: In February 2026, I identified a new phishing campaign associated with MuddyWater, framed as a travel reservation from Air Arabia. When recipients enable the document's embedded macro, it installs and executes the GhostFetch loader. This post analyses the campaign's lure design, delivery mechanism, and GhostFetch behaviour, and provides practical guidance for defenders.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
MuddyWater (also tracked as UNC5667, Earth Vetala, Mango Sandstorm, MUDDYCOAST, Seedworm, and TA450) is an Iranian state-aligned APT group operating on behalf of Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). Active since at least 2017, the group primarily targets government, telecommunications, energy, and financial sector organisations across the Middle East, North Africa, and South Asia.1 MuddyWater consistently relies on macro-enabled Office documents as initial access vectors, combined with staged payload reconstruction and business-themed lures tailored to regional targets.

GhostFetch is a first-stage downloader attributed to MuddyWater, publicly documented by Group-IB as part of Operation Olalampo — a campaign first observed on 26 January 2026 targeting organisations across the MENA region.2 GhostFetch performs environmental evasion checks before fetching and reflectively loading secondary payloads in memory, ultimately delivering GhostBackDoor — a second-stage implant that provides interactive shell access, file manipulation, and AES-encrypted C2 communications through French-named API endpoints.3 The analysis here was conducted independently and predates Group-IB's public reporting, allowing for cross-referencing against their findings on the delivered GhostBackDoor implant.

docs.title: Reservation Document Lure Analysis
docs.text:
I identified a malicious Word document associated with MuddyWater uploaded to VirusTotal from the UAE on 30 January 2026. The file, titled "Sajeev Saliha Beevi.doc," masquerades as a legitimate Air Arabia reservation itinerary. The document embeds detailed booking information, including the reservation number, flight routes between Abu Dhabi (AUH) and Thiruvananthapuram (TRV), passenger details, and travel agent information. Its professional formatting and realistic travel metadata indicate that the lure was crafted to appear operationally authentic.

Although the original delivery mechanism remains unknown, the content suggests MuddyWater aimed this document at individuals or organisations with ties to the UAE travel corridor — including corporate travel coordinators, finance departments, and business travelers.

Exhibit 1: Weaponised Lure Word Document

The document's metadata further supports attribution to MuddyWater and aligns with the group's established operational practices. The file lists "DontAsk" as the author and "FireToRain" as the last saving user, with Microsoft Office Word as the originating application. The document contains 10 recorded revisions with an approximate total editing time of six minutes. The "Content created" timestamp of 25 January 2026 at 12:52 AM and "Date last saved" timestamp of 26 January 2026 at 11:55 AM indicate a compressed preparation window of roughly 24–72 hours before deployment.

This pattern is consistent with MuddyWater operational workflows observed across multiple campaigns. Earlier reporting identified lure documents authored on Windows systems and saved under operator-associated usernames including "jojo" and "phoenix". Taken together, the metadata artefacts, lure construction, and macro-based execution workflow support a moderate to high confidence assessment that the document reflects established MuddyWater tradecraft.

Exhibit 2: Weaponised Lure Word Document Metadata

While the document appears benign to the end user, technical analysis reveals embedded VBA macros configured to execute automatically when the file opens. The macro functions as a first-stage dropper — it reconstructs an encoded Windows PE file embedded within a "UserForm" object, writes the payload to disk, and executes it.

docs.title: VBA Macro Analysis
docs.text:
The macro is designed to execute when the document opens in Microsoft Word with macros permitted — either through explicit user consent or in environments where macro security controls are disabled or insufficiently enforced.

Once triggered, the macro initiates a staged execution sequence that reconstructs and deploys a concealed second-stage payload embedded within the document. The malicious logic resides entirely within the VBA project. When opened in the Word VBA editor, the VBA project appears password protected.

Exhibit 3: Password Protected VBA Project

However, extraction of the VBA streams confirms that the primary execution logic resides within the "ThisDocument" class module.

Exhibit 4: Word Document Stream Dump

The macro implements a staged workflow. It first calls a delay function (wait()), likely to impede automated analysis. It then retrieves a numerically encoded string from UserForm1.TextBox1.Text and decodes it in three-digit increments to reconstruct a Windows Portable Executable (PE) payload.

If the payload does not already exist on disk, the macro writes the decoded content to C:\Users\Public\Documents\MicrosoftWordUser.log, renames it to MicrosoftWordUser.exe, and executes it via ShellExecute. This sequence functions as a self-contained dropper that reconstructs and launches the embedded second-stage payload.

Exhibit 5: Staged Macro Dropper

The numerically encoded string retrieved from UserForm1.TextBox1.Text serves as the embedded payload container. The associated UserForm1/o stream contains a large sequence of decimal values.

Exhibit 6: UserForm1/o Stream Content

The macro's decoding routine processes this string in three-character increments, converting each three-digit value into its corresponding ASCII byte to reconstruct the raw binary payload in memory.

Exhibit 7: Staged Macro Dropper Decoding Routine Exhibit 8: "MZ" Signature that Identifies a Windows Portable Executable (PE) File

Before writing and executing the reconstructed executable, the macro checks for the presence of MicrosoftWordUser.exe using the Dir() function, preventing redundant deployment. It writes the payload as MicrosoftWordUser.log, renames it to MicrosoftWordUser.exe, then instantiates the Shell.Application COM object and invokes ShellExecute to launch the renamed executable.

Exhibit 9: Conditional File Write and Execution Logic

In summary: when Document_Open() triggers, the macro introduces artificial delays, decodes the numerically encoded payload from a UserForm stream, writes it to C:\Users\Public\Documents\MicrosoftWordUser.log, renames it to MicrosoftWordUser.exe, and executes it via Shell.Application.

docs.title: GhostFetch Analysis
docs.text:
The executable dropped by the VBA macro is GhostFetch — the first-stage downloader documented by Group-IB as part of Operation Olalampo.2 Unlike the macro, which functions solely as a delivery mechanism, GhostFetch implements a multi-stage execution flow covering environmental evasion, persistence installation, and encrypted C2 communication. Static analysis identifies it as a 64-bit Windows PE compiled using Microsoft Visual C++.

Exhibit 10: DIE (Detect it Easy) Static Analysis Metadata Output

docs.title: Anti-Analysis / Anti-Debugging / VM Detection
docs.text:
Before any persistence or network activity begins, GhostFetch runs an anti-debugging check at FUN_140006080. It first inspects the Process Environment Block (PEB), checking the BeingDebugged flag and NtGlobalFlag. If either indicates a debugger is present, GhostFetch immediately exits.

Exhibit 11: PEB Checks and NtQueryInformationProcess Resolution

GhostFetch performs a screen resolution check at FUN_140004190 as an additional sandbox and VM detection layer. The function calls GetMonitorInfoW to retrieve display dimensions, then compares them against a hardcoded whitelist of width and height combinations. Valid widths are 1440, 1920, and 2560 pixels; valid heights are 900, 1080, 1200, and 1600 pixels. If the detected resolution does not match any expected combination, GhostFetch sets an abort flag — sandbox environments and VMs commonly run at atypical resolutions such as 800×600 or 1024×768.

Exhibit 12: Screen Resolution Check Exhibit 13: GetMonitorInfoW Function Call Exhibit 14: Screen Resolution Detection Validation Logic

GhostFetch also implements a composite sandbox detection routine at FUN_140004260, invoked only if the screen resolution check has already flagged the environment as suspicious. Rather than relying on a single indicator, the function combines three independent hardware checks and returns 1 to trigger abort only if all three conditions are simultaneously true — minimising false positives on real endpoints.

Exhibit 15: Conditional Execution Chain

The three checks are: logical processor count (fewer than two CPUs flags as sandbox), total physical RAM (less than 2 GB flags as sandbox), and USB device history via the Windows registry (fewer than two historically connected devices flags as sandbox).

Exhibit 16: Sandbox Fingerprinting Logic Exhibit 17: Composite Return Logic

GhostFetch enumerates all running processes and compares them against a hardcoded list of security tools and analysis frameworks. If any listed process is detected, execution aborts immediately. The enumeration operates in two phases: a targeted check for antivirus product processes, followed by runtime decoding of obfuscated analysis tool names.

Exhibit 18: AV Detection ("avp.exe" — Kaspersky Anti-Virus process)

The complete list of targeted processes covers every major category of analysis tooling — debuggers (ollydbg.exe, immunitydebugger.exe, windbg.exe, x32dbg.exe, x64dbg.exe), disassemblers (ida.exe, ida64.exe, idaq.exe, ida664.exe, pestudio.exe), dynamic instrumentation (frida-helper-32.exe, frida-helper-64.exe), process inspection tools (processhacker.exe, procexp.exe, procmon.exe), network analysis tools (wireshark.exe, fiddler.exe, httpdebugger.exe), and sandbox platforms (joeboxcontrol.exe, joeboxserver.exe).

Exhibit 19: Example Runtime Decoding of Obfuscated Process Name ("ollydbg.exe")

docs.title: Mouse Logging
docs.text:
GhostFetch implements a system-wide mouse logging capability at FUN_1400040c0. The function installs a low-level mouse hook using SetWindowsHookExW with hook type 0xE (WH_MOUSE_LL), intercepting all mouse events system-wide — clicks, movements, and scroll wheel input — before they reach any application.

Exhibit 20: Mouse Hook via SetWindowsHookExW Exhibit 21: GetMessageW Message Pump Loop Maintaining the Mouse Hook Exhibit 22: DefWindowProcW Message Pump Loop Maintaining the Mouse Hook

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
After successful execution, GhostFetch installs a persistent copy of itself at %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\BurnUtill\burn.exe. Both the directory name and subdirectory structure are reconstructed at runtime from obfuscated short arrays decoded through a per-position subtraction scheme. The self-copy logic first decodes the target directory path, creates it if absent, opens the running executable for reading, copies the PE image into a heap-allocated buffer, and writes the result to the decoded destination path.

Exhibit 23: Runtime Construction of the "burn.exe" Destination Path

docs.title: C2 Infrastructure
docs.text:
The analysed sample maintains a hardcoded list of 20 C2 hosts. The primary entry, promoverse[.]org, is stored in plaintext and embedded directly in the binary as raw character bytes with no obfuscation.

Exhibit 24: C2 Domain (promoverse[.]org)

The full C2 request URL hxxps://promoverse[.]org/api/debut is assembled at runtime from three components stored separately in the binary. The host appears as raw character bytes; the URL path /api/debut is stored as an encoded short integer array decoded using the same XOR-based decoder used for other obfuscated strings. All three components are passed to WinHttpOpenRequest at runtime.

Exhibit 25: "/api/debut" URL Path

The remaining 19 C2 entries are lightly encoded — each stored as a byte sequence recovered at runtime by adding a fixed numeric offset. In the analysed sample, all 19 decode to invalid placeholder strings following the pattern 999.999.999.999x, counting down from 9998 to 9980. This is inconsistent with real operator infrastructure and strongly suggests the binary was compiled with generated placeholder values. The slots can hold up to 16-character strings, and the presence of promoverse[.]org in slot zero confirms the mechanism can store domain names.

Exhibit 26: Decoded C2 / Placeholder Entries

As this analysis was being finalised, Group-IB published their Operation Olalampo report independently documenting the same loader and including a retrieval of the encrypted second-stage payload from promoverse[.]org.2 This timing allowed cross-referencing their findings on the delivered GhostBackDoor implant against static analysis, filling the one gap that could not be resolved from the binary alone.

According to Group-IB, GhostBackDoor functions as a second-stage implant that adapts its persistence mechanism based on available system privileges — often masquerading as the Windows Recycle Bin ClassID or establishing itself as a service named MicrosoftVersionUpdater. Once reflectively loaded into memory, the backdoor facilitates interactive shell access and file manipulation through AES-encrypted communications with French-named API endpoints, purposefully fragmenting network traffic into separate requests to evade behavioural detection.3

docs.title: From Invoice Lure to In-Memory Injection: Phantom Stealer via Donut and Heaven's Gate
From Invoice Lure to In-Memory Injection
docs.text: In January 2026, I identified a phishing campaign leveraging compromised supplier mailboxes and a multi-stage infection chain to deploy Phantom Stealer using obfuscated batch loaders, in-memory PowerShell decryption, Donut shellcode injection, and Heaven's Gate evasion. This post analyses the campaign's tradecraft, persistence mechanisms, and data exfiltration methods.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
Phantom Stealer is a commodity information-stealing malware family marketed within underground forums as a stealer-as-a-service (SaaS) offering. Proofpoint researchers have documented significant code overlap between Phantom Stealer and Stealerium — an open-source stealer project — with Phantom Stealer representing one of several derivatives built on that codebase.1 The malware targets browser-stored credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, FTP clients, email applications, and session tokens from platforms such as Discord and Telegram. HP's December 2025 Threat Insights Report identified Phantom Stealer as one of several purchasable malware kits being actively weaponised by threat actors to evade detection through regularly updated evasion modules.2

Donut is an open-source shellcode generation framework that converts .NET assemblies, native executables, and scripts into position-independent shellcode executable entirely in memory, without touching disk.3 Its legitimate use in red team operations has made it a common fixture in commodity malware chains seeking to bypass file-based AV detection.

Heaven's Gate is an evasion technique that exploits the Windows on Windows 64-bit (WoW64) compatibility layer to execute 64-bit code from within a 32-bit process. First documented around 2009, it has since been adopted by a range of malware families — including FormBook4 and ACRStealer5 — to bypass user-mode API hooks that endpoint security products place on the 32-bit Windows API layer.

docs.title: Key Highlights
docs.text:
• Threat actors leveraged previously compromised supplier email accounts to distribute phishing messages, increasing credibility and bypassing trust-based controls
  • The campaign employed an obfuscated Batch loader, embedded Base64 PowerShell payload, AES decryption, and in-memory shellcode injection into explorer.exe to avoid disk-based detection
  • Phantom Stealer implemented WoW64 architectural mode switching to execute 64-bit code from a 32-bit process, bypassing user-mode API hooks and complicating endpoint monitoring
  • Stolen credentials, wallet data, and session artefacts were compressed, transmitted via Telegram or Discord infrastructure, and followed by local artefact cleanup to reduce forensic visibility

docs.title: Campaign Analysis
docs.text:
In January 2026, I observed a phishing campaign targeting companies across multiple industry sectors. The campaign uses deceptive procurement-themed lures to trick employees into interacting with malicious attachments, delivering Phantom Stealer through a multi-stage attachment chain.

Notably, attackers abused seemingly legitimate supplier accounts as sending infrastructure — sender mailboxes were likely compromised prior to the phishing activity. The campaign uniquely leveraged compromised accounts originating from the United Arab Emirates and Qatar. In some cases, the same company was targeted with several different lures, all designed to deliver the same Phantom Stealer payload.

This campaign is not isolated. In December 2025, security researchers documented Operation MoneyMount-ISO — a campaign targeting financial services, accounting, procurement, legal, and HR functions — which used fake payment confirmation emails with malicious ISO attachments to deploy Phantom Stealer, exfiltrating data via Telegram bots and Discord webhooks.6

Recipient domain analysis indicates targeting across industrial manufacturing, engineering, agricultural export, chemicals, and energy-related sectors in Europe and Asia.

Exhibit 1: Phishing Samples Observed

docs.title: First Stage: Batch Dropper
docs.text:
The attached compressed file contains a Windows Batch script executed once the archive is opened and the file is launched. The script is heavily padded with randomised variable assignments and meaningless arithmetic operations intended to obscure the script's true behaviour and delay manual analysis.

Upon execution, the Batch file relaunches itself in a minimised window to reduce user visibility and copies its own contents into a newly created directory under the user's roaming AppData path. It then establishes persistence by adding a registry value under the current user's Run key, ensuring the malicious Batch file executes automatically at each login.

After establishing persistence, the script prepares a secondary payload embedded directly within the Batch file itself — no external retrieval required. The embedded payload is located on the final line of the Batch file, prefixed with the distinctive marker string ::M0SjGsVxEzjdf formatted as a Batch comment, making it invisible during normal script execution.

Exhibit 2: Attached ".bat" File

The script reads its own contents using PowerShell, searches for the marker to identify the start of the encoded data, extracts everything following it, and treats it as Base64 encoded content. This data is decoded and written to %TEMP%\continue.ps1 — referenced in the script via the variable UNIVERSE.

The file is then executed immediately using PowerShell with a hidden window and execution policy bypass. Following execution of the decoded PowerShell payload, the temporary script file is deleted to minimise residual artefacts on disk.

docs.title: Second Stage: PowerShell Payload and In-Memory Injection
docs.text:
The PowerShell code is the second-stage loader responsible for decrypting, injecting, and executing the primary malicious component entirely in memory. It transitions execution from script-based logic into native code by preparing an encrypted payload for runtime decryption and remote execution within a legitimate Windows process.

The script begins by collecting basic host context through environment variables and enforcing single-instance execution via a named mutex using System.Threading.Mutex. An attempt is made to open an existing mutex named CRACKHONOR_Mtx — if it already exists, execution terminates immediately, preventing multiple concurrent instances. The script then verifies the presence of a running explorer.exe process and retrieves the associated PID, exiting if a valid target cannot be identified.

Exhibit 3: PowerShell Payload (Beginning of File)

The embedded payload is stored as a large Base64 blob, decoded and decrypted at runtime using the .NET cryptography framework. Decryption uses AES in CBC mode with PKCS7 padding. The encryption key is derived by computing the SHA-256 hash of a hardcoded passphrase, while the initialisation vector is statically defined and decoded from a Base64 string. Once decrypted, the resulting byte array represents raw executable code for in-memory execution.

To execute this payload, the script dynamically compiles inline C# using Add-Type to expose native Windows API functions from kernel32.dll.

Exhibit 4: Native API Injection Setup via Add-Type

The injection sequence uses OpenProcess to obtain a handle to explorer.exe, VirtualAllocEx to allocate remote memory, WriteProcessMemory to copy the decrypted payload, VirtualProtectEx to mark memory as executable, and CreateRemoteThread to transfer execution. The payload executes entirely within explorer.exe's address space without ever being written to disk as a standalone executable.

After successful injection, the script enters a persistent monitoring loop — if explorer.exe terminates or restarts, the script repeats the injection routine against the new instance, ensuring continued execution across process restarts.

docs.title: Third Stage: Donut Shellcode Loader
docs.text:
The decrypted payload injected into explorer.exe is position-independent shellcode generated using Donut version 0.9.2.3 This shellcode serves as the third stage and is responsible for unpacking and executing the final payload — a .NET assembly identified as Phantom Stealer.

The AES key was derived from the SHA-256 hash of the passphrase restore_31_phazzy Lee, with the initialisation vector decoded from the embedded Base64 value S+hKtckT2gd+1tyosBp/LA==.

Exhibit 5: Shellcode Donut Loader

The shellcode structure follows the documented Donut framework architecture. Execution begins with a relative CALL instruction at offset zero that jumps over approximately 600 kilobytes of encrypted payload data to reach the unpacker stub at offset 0x9329D.

Exhibit 6: Donut Shellcode Entry Point

API resolution is performed entirely without import table entries through PEB traversal, matching the implementation in Donut's /peb.c source file. The function at offset 0x9612D accesses the Thread Environment Block via the GS segment register, walks to the PEB loader data structures, and enumerates loaded modules to locate required DLLs.

Exhibit 7: PEB Walking Function

For each dependency, the loader parses the PE export directory and computes a hash of exported function names for comparison against precomputed values embedded in the shellcode configuration.

Exhibit 8: PE Export Parser Function Exhibit 9: DLL Extension Appending Logic

docs.title: Phantom Stealer Analysis
docs.text:
Exhibit 10: Phantom Stealer Advertised Offers

Beyond standard obfuscation, the analysed sample incorporates advanced runtime evasion that distinguishes it from typical commodity stealers. Static analysis of the extracted .NET assembly reveals a class named HeavensGate within the Stub namespace, indicating the malware implements architectural mode switching to circumvent endpoint security monitoring.

docs.title: Heaven's Gate: Architectural Mode Switching
docs.text:
The Heaven's Gate technique exploits the WoW64 compatibility layer to execute 64-bit code from within a 32-bit process. The fundamental principle relies on the fact that 32-bit processes running under WoW64 are hosted within a native 64-bit process, with the 64-bit ntdll.dll loaded at initialisation. Security products that instrument only the 32-bit ntdll.dll remain blind to system calls issued directly through the 64-bit layer.

The HeavensGate class first verifies execution within a 32-bit process context, then resolves critical functions from the 64-bit ntdll.dll — including LdrLoadDll, LdrUnloadDll, LdrGetDllHandle, and LdrGetProcedureAddress — through custom PEB traversal routines implemented in the Utils64 helper class. A static boolean field named operational gates all subsequent 64-bit execution attempts.

Exhibit 11: Heaven's Gate Initialization Resolving 64-bit NTDLL Exports

The core implementation resides in the Execute64 method and its associated shellcode stub stored in the Wow64ExecuteShellCode byte array.

Exhibit 12: Shellcode Stub Performing x86 to x64 Code Segment Transition

This shellcode performs the critical code segment register manipulation — switching from the 32-bit segment selector 0x23 to the 64-bit selector 0x33 through a far jump instruction, then transitioning back to 32-bit mode after execution completes. This allows Phantom Stealer to call 64-bit versions of LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress, loading and invoking functions from 64-bit DLLs while evading any monitoring hooks present in the 32-bit execution layer.

Exhibit 13: Dynamic 64-bit Shellcode Generation Following Windows x64 Calling Convention

docs.title: Data Exfiltration via Telegram Bot API
docs.text:
Phantom Stealer uses the Telegram Bot API as its primary exfiltration channel — a technique increasingly favoured by commodity stealers due to its reliability, encryption in transit, and the difficulty defenders face in blocking legitimate Telegram infrastructure without disrupting business operations.

The TelegramSendLogs class implements the complete exfiltration workflow. The SendReportAsync method orchestrates upload of harvested data files through the UploadToTelegram helper class before transmitting a formatted summary message.

After upload, the malware attempts to delete local evidence — removing .txt, .png, and .json files from its working directory as a basic anti-forensics measure. The Telegram bot token and chat identifier are stored in the Config class and retrieved through StringsCrypt.DecryptConfig, which decrypts ENCRYPTED:BncRbgTGet4L+mKqD8dz7h8EdEcrI2Pbm5InYO5Ff/I= at runtime to reveal the base API endpoint.

Exhibit 14: Telegram Exfiltration Workflow with Post-upload Evidence Deletion

The SendMessageInfoAsync method constructs a detailed victim profile in Telegram's Markdown parsing mode, including Windows version, username, computer name, detected antivirus product, gateway IP, internal IP, and external IP. The report provides a statistical breakdown of harvested data by type — passwords, credit cards, cookies, browser wallet extensions, desktop cryptocurrency wallets, FTP credentials, VPN accounts, and session data from Outlook, FoxMail, Telegram, Discord, and WinScp.

Configuration flags indicating whether persistence, keylogging, screenshot capture, clipboard hijacking, and file grabbing modules are active are appended, giving the operator full visibility of implant capabilities. Notably, the message footer contains direct attribution to the malware author via the Telegram handle Oldphantomoftheopera and the marketing website phantomsoftwares[.]site, confirming the stealer-as-a-service distribution model.

Exhibit 15: Phantom Stealer Author Indicators Embedded in Exfiltration Payload

docs.title: Malicious Distribution of RMM Tools via Adobe-Themed Download Infrastructure
docs.text:
In March and April 2026, I observed a some spearphishing samples that were most likely a part of a phishing campaign targeting financial departments in Europe and across multiple sectors. The campaign directed victims to previously compromised websites hosting fake Adobe software that deployed Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) tools to establish access to victim systems. In one observed case, the phishing email, purporting to be a document pending to be signed, was delivered to the victim mailbox, passing email security filters (Exhibit 1).

Exhibit 1: Phishing Email Received by the Victim

docs.title: Initial Access: Phishing Email Analysis
docs.text:
The email contained a hyperlink purporting to direct the recipient to an Adobe document awaiting signature, with the sender impersonating "Adobe Acrobat Sign." The message leveraged Adobe trademarks and branding elements, increasing the likelihood that the email would appear legitimate to recipients.

Looking at the raw email headers, the sender domain hpgrp[.]com was spoofed. The headers also expose 153.127.234[.]4 as part of the message delivery path — an IP I have observed in several phishing campaigns dating back to early 2025, suggesting the attacker reuses infrastructure across related operations.

docs.title: Delivery: Fake Adobe Download Page
docs.text:
Upon clicking the "Access your Complete Document" button, the victim is redirected to echo-resorts[.]com/adobe/, where a message claims that their Adobe version has expired (Exhibit 2). The page then triggers an automatic fake Adobe software download without requiring further user interaction (Exhibit 3).

Exhibit 2: Fraudulent warning message

Exhibit 3: Automatically Downloaded Fake Adobe Software

docs.title: Payload: SuperOps RMM Agent
docs.text:
On execution the file does not install any Adobe product. Instead it kicks off the setup wizard for SuperOps (Exhibit 4) — a legitimate RMM platform developed by Superops Inc. and designed for Managed Service Providers (MSPs) to remotely monitor, manage, and control client endpoints. SuperOps RMM gives the operator remote shell access, file transfer, arbitrary command execution, software deployment, and real-time system monitoring. While intended for legitimate IT administration, RMM tools have become an increasingly favoured vector for threat actors — full remote access through trusted, digitally signed binaries that endpoint security solutions tend to whitelist by default.

Exhibit 4: SuperOps RMM setup wizard

docs.title: MSI Payload Analysis
docs.text: I pulled the MSI apart and assess that the threat actor registered a SuperOps.ai RMM account, getting a tenant on the European production infrastructure. SuperOps offers a 14-day free trial that gives full agent generation, including the ability to download pre-configured MSI installers — no identity check, no payment. The MSI itself is a stock SuperOps build: legitimately signed with a valid Sectigo code signing certificate issued to Superops Inc. (Delaware, US), and no modifications in the agent binary itself (Exhibit 5).

docs.title: Certificate Details
docs.text: Field Value Name Superops Inc. Status Valid Issuer Sectigo Public Code Signing CA R36 Valid From 12:00 AM 04/14/2023 Valid To 11:59 PM 07/13/2026 Thumbprint CBF98AFF4D4BD00B83018D60ABE11DDF95C34664 Serial Number 3E 4F 07 83 9D 57 49 85 80 4D A5 5C 80 B5 D9 C0 > Exhibit 5: SuperOps RMM Certificate Details

docs.title: Tenant Authentication via Filename
docs.text:
SuperOps embeds tenant authentication credentials directly in the MSI filename. When an MSP generates an agent installer from the SuperOps platform, the resulting filename follows the convention:

<prefix>_<tenantID_base36>_<siteID_base36>_<platform>_<architecture>.msi

Exhibit 6: SuperOps Application Naming Convention

The MSI's internal "Custom Action" table confirms the installer reads its own filepath at execution time and extracts the filename to authenticate the installation to the correct tenant account. The MSI even enforces filename integrity with the warning: "Please make sure the file name is not altered and used as it is downloaded from the site." SuperOps' own documentation backs this up: "Do not rename the .msi and .pkg agent files, as the system will not be able to recognize the installed agent" (Exhibit 7).

Exhibit 7: SuperOps Documentation Regarding TenantID and SessionID

The catch is that the installer only actually validates the tenant and site ID positions within the filename (positions [len-4] and [len-3] from the underscore-delimited segments). The first segment — the prefix — is not validated and can be freely modified without breaking the installer. The threat actor abused this by replacing the default prefix with "Adobe", producing the filename Adobe_1M021SDPX2OZK_19SI0B7FBSUF4_windows_x64.msi.

docs.title: Execution Flow
docs.text: On execution, the MSI's Custom Action DLL extracts the filename from the MSI's filepath on disk, then launches the embedded Go binary (superopssetup.exe) with the full filename passed as a command-line argument. The binary decodes the tenant and site IDs and registers the victim's machine with the attacker's SuperOps account.

docs.title: C2 Infrastructure
docs.text:
The binary's embedded configuration is SERVER_LOCATION=EU and SERVER_TYPE=PROD, targeting the European production C2 infrastructure. The C2 endpoints are:

Endpoint Value RMM Server euagent.superops[.]ai Lambda API lambdaapi.superopsmsp[.]com WebSocket ws.superopsmsp[.]com Registration Endpoint POST euagent.superops[.]ai/rmm-web/rmm/getInstallerInfoForRegAsset

docs.title: Abuse of RMM Tools in the Wild
docs.text:
The abuse of RMM tools by threat actors is well documented and growing. In January 2023 CISA, NSA, and MS-ISAC issued joint advisory AA23-025A specifically warning of the malicious use of legitimate RMM software delivered via phishing. SuperOps in particular has been linked to multiple campaigns:

  • In May 2024, CERT-UA identified threat actor UAC-0188 delivering SuperOps RMM to financial institutions in the US and Europe via trojanised Minesweeper clones.
  • In January 2026, ASEC documented ongoing campaigns distributing SuperOps, Syncro, NinjaOne, and ScreenConnect RMM tools disguised as PDF invoices, noting that these tools have been previously associated with ransomware operators including Chaos, Royal, ALPHV/BlackCat, Hive, and Lunar Spider, as well as the Iranian APT group MuddyWater.
  • ThreatDown has identified SuperOps abuse by the CACTUS ransomware group.
  • In December 2025, SuperOps published a statement acknowledging the misuse and confirming it originated from illegitimate accounts.

At this stage I couldn't pin the activity on a specific actor based purely on the payload — the TTPs are consistent with the broader RMM abuse trend documented across multiple sources. So I went hunting on the infrastructure side instead.

docs.title: Discovery of the Phishing Page Source Code
docs.text:
I pivoted on the observed network infrastructure — suspicious download URLs, hosting patterns, and the Adobe-themed lure paths used to push the RMM agents — which surfaced a number of additional domains tied to the same delivery infrastructure.

I also saw multiple RMM tools in play. On top of the SuperOps and ConnectWise observations, the broader infrastructure and lure patterns suggested distribution of other legitimate RMM software like ITarian, Atera, and SimpleHelp — which lines up with the wider trend of threat actors leaning on legitimate administrative tooling for remote access and persistence.
